rationale: The speaker asks God to guide his speech and reflection; God similarly promises Moses to open his mouth and teach what he should say.
source_text: May God grant me to speak with judgment and to reflect worthily on what has been given, for He is both the guide of wisdom and the corrector of the wise.

target_units.text: The Lord said to Moses, “Who gave a human being a mouth? Who made one hard of hearing or deaf, seeing or blind? Is it not I, God?
Now therefore go, and I will open your mouth, and teach you what you are to speak.”

relationship: close divine-hand dependence of the wise
rationale: Wisdom places people, words and understanding in God's hand; Ecclesiastes likewise puts the righteous, wise and their works in God's hand.
source_text: For in His hand are both we and our words, all understanding and skill in crafts.

target_units.text: For I set all this upon my heart, and my heart saw all this: the righteous, the wise and their works are in God’s hand. A person knows neither love nor hatred; everything lies before them.

relationship: related divine wisdom and the ordered natural world
rationale: God-given knowledge of the world's composition corresponds to Job's depiction of God knowing wisdom and ordering winds, waters and rain.
source_text: For He Himself gave me unerring knowledge of existing things: to know the composition of the world and the activity of the elements,

target_units.text: God established its way well, and He knows its place.
For He observes the whole realm under heaven, knowing everything in the earth that He made:
the weight of winds and measures of water;
when He acted in this way, He counted rain and a path for sounds amid a shaking.
Then He saw wisdom and expounded it; having prepared it, He traced it out.

relationship: creation background for knowledge of times
rationale: The knowledge of seasons and temporal divisions concerns the calendar that Genesis assigns to the heavenly lights for signs, seasons, days and years.
source_text: the beginning and end and middle of times, the changes of the solstices and the transitions of seasons,

target_units.text: And God said, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to give light upon the earth and to divide the day from the night. Let them serve for signs and seasons, for days and years.

relationship: creation background for stellar and yearly order
rationale: Knowledge of yearly cycles and star positions corresponds to the lights and stars appointed in Genesis to govern temporal and celestial order.
source_text: the cycles of the year and the positions of stars,

target_units.text: And God said, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to give light upon the earth and to divide the day from the night. Let them serve for signs and seasons, for days and years.
And let them be lights in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth.” And it was so.
And God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night; He made the stars also.
And God set them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth,
to rule the day and the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good.

relationship: Solomonic natural-knowledge parallel
rationale: Wisdom lists knowledge of creatures and plants; Kings likewise describes Solomon speaking about trees, livestock, birds, creeping things and fish, without supplying all the other fields listed here.
source_text: the natures of living creatures and the tempers of wild animals, the forces of winds and the reasonings of human beings, the varieties of plants and the powers of roots.

target_units.text: He spoke about trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing through the wall. He spoke about livestock, birds, creeping things, and fish.

relationship: parallel wisdom's relation to all created works
rationale: Wisdom is the artisan of all things and the speaker's teacher; the psalm likewise attributes God's manifold works to wisdom.
source_text: I learned all that is hidden and manifest, for wisdom, the artisan of all things, taught me.

target_units.text: How great Thy works have become, Lord! Thou madest all things in wisdom; the earth was filled with Thy possession.

relationship: related description of pure wisdom
rationale: Wisdom's intelligent, holy and undefiled spirit corresponds to James's description of heavenly wisdom as first pure and then morally beneficent; the lists are not identical.
source_text: For in her is a spirit intelligent, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, agile, lucid, undefiled, clear, unharmed, loving the good, keen,

target_units.text: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, considerate, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, without hypocrisy.

relationship: internal expansion of wisdom's benevolent universal spirit
rationale: The spirit that loves humanity and oversees all develops the opening description of wisdom's human-loving spirit and the world-filling Spirit's knowledge.
source_text: unhindered, beneficent, loving humanity, steadfast, secure, free from care, all-powerful, all-overseeing, and passing through all spirits that are intelligent, pure, and most subtle.

target_units.text: For wisdom is a spirit that loves humanity, and she will not acquit a blasphemer of what his lips have said; for God is a witness of his kidneys, a true overseer of his heart, and a hearer of his tongue.
For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world, and that which holds all things together has knowledge of utterance.

relationship: internal parallel of wisdom's universal reach
rationale: Wisdom's penetration of all things corresponds to her mighty reach from end to end and governance of all things.
source_text: For wisdom is more mobile than every motion; she penetrates and passes through all things because of her purity.

target_units.text: She reaches mightily from end to end, and governs all things well.

relationship: related divine-glory emanation imagery
rationale: Wisdom is a pure outflow of God's glory; Hebrews describes the Son as the radiance of His glory. The relationship concerns shared imagery, without claiming the verse explicitly identifies Wisdom as the Son.
source_text: For she is a breath of God’s power and a pure outflow of the Almighty’s glory; therefore nothing defiled enters into her.

target_units.text: He is the radiance of His glory and the imprint of His being, upholding all things by the word of His power. Having made purification of sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,

relationship: close radiance-and-image imagery
rationale: Wisdom is radiance of eternal light and an image of divine goodness; Hebrews calls the Son radiance of glory and imprint of God's being, a literary-theological parallel with distinct formulations.
source_text: For she is a radiance of eternal light, an unstained mirror of God’s activity, and an image of His goodness.

target_units.text: He is the radiance of His glory and the imprint of His being, upholding all things by the word of His power. Having made purification of sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,

relationship: related renewal through divine spiritual agency
rationale: Wisdom renews all things while passing into holy souls; the psalm connects the sending of God's Spirit with creation and renewal of the earth, without supplying the prophet-making detail.
source_text: Though she is one, she can do all things; remaining in herself, she renews all things, and passing into holy souls from generation to generation, she makes friends of God and prophets.

target_units.text: Thou wilt send Thy Spirit, and they will be created, and Thou wilt renew the face of the earth.

relationship: related divine love and faithful indwelling
rationale: God loves the one dwelling with wisdom; Jesus likewise promises the Father's love and divine dwelling to those keeping His word.
source_text: For God loves no one except the one who dwells with wisdom.

target_units.text: The one who has My commandments and keeps them is the one who loves Me. And the one who loves Me will be loved by My Father, and I will love him and reveal Myself to him.”
Judas—not the Iscariot—says to Him, “Lord, what then has happened that Thou art going to reveal Thyself to us and not to the world?”
Jesus answered and said to him, “If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word, and My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our dwelling with him.

relationship: explicit same-chapter comparison of wisdom with light
rationale: Wisdom's superiority to sun, stars and light supplies the basis for the speaker's earlier choice of her over light.
source_text: For she is more beautiful than the sun and surpasses every arrangement of stars; compared with light, she is found superior.

target_units.text: I loved her more than health and beauty, and chose to have her rather than light, because the radiance that comes from her never sleeps.

relationship: related unconquered-light motif
rationale: Wisdom's superiority to alternating daylight is expressed as evil's failure to overpower her; John similarly says darkness did not overcome the light, with its own account of the Word.
source_text: For night succeeds light, but evil does not overpower wisdom.

target_units.text: And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.

relationship: internal parallel of universal ordered governance
rationale: Wisdom governs all things well from end to end; the later prayer describes God arranging all things by measure, number and weight.
source_text: She reaches mightily from end to end, and governs all things well.

target_units.text: Even without these, they could have fallen at a single breath, pursued by justice and winnowed away by the breath of Thy power; but Thou didst arrange all things by measure and number and weight.

relationship: related personification of wisdom as intimate companion
rationale: Wisdom is sought as a bride here; Proverbs asks the learner to call wisdom a sister and understanding a familiar companion, using different family images for close attachment.
source_text: I loved her and sought her out from my youth, and sought to take her as my bride, and became a lover of her beauty.

target_units.text: Say that wisdom is your sister, and acquire understanding as your familiar companion,

relationship: parallel divine delight in companion wisdom
rationale: Wisdom's shared life with God and the Master's love correspond to Proverbs' Wisdom beside God as the one in whom He delighted.
source_text: She glorifies her noble birth by sharing life with God, and the Master of all loved her;

target_units.text: I was beside Him, fitting things together; I was the one in whom He delighted. Day by day I rejoiced before Him at every time,

relationship: parallel wisdom's participation in divine works
rationale: Wisdom knows God and His works here; Proverbs depicts her present beside Him as the heavens and earth are ordered.
source_text: for she is initiated into God’s knowledge and is a chooser of His works.

target_units.text: When He was preparing heaven, I was present with Him, and when He was marking out His own throne upon winds.
When He was making the clouds above strong, and when He was setting the springs of the world beneath heaven secure,
and was making the foundations of the earth strong,
I was beside Him, fitting things together; I was the one in whom He delighted. Day by day I rejoiced before Him at every time,

relationship: parallel wisdom as source of richer possessions
rationale: Wisdom surpasses wealth because she works all things; Proverbs likewise associates her with wealth, righteousness and storehouses filled for those who love her.
source_text: If wealth is a desirable possession in life, what is richer than wisdom, who works all things?

target_units.text: Wealth and glory belong to me, and possession of many things and righteousness.
It is better to reap me than gold and precious stone, and my produce is better than choice silver.
I walk in ways of righteousness, and move in the midst of paths of just judgment,
so that I may apportion substance to those who love me, and fill their storehouses with good things.

relationship: related incomparable creative wisdom
rationale: Wisdom's unsurpassed skill corresponds to the wisdom by which God founded the earth and prepared the heavens.
source_text: And if understanding accomplishes things, who among existing beings is more skilled than she?

target_units.text: God founded the earth by wisdom and prepared the heavens by good sense.

relationship: parallel wisdom producing moral and governing virtues
rationale: Wisdom teaches self-control, understanding, righteousness and courage; Proverbs assigns her understanding, strength and righteous judgment, a related but not identical enumeration.
source_text: And if anyone loves righteousness, her labors are virtues; for she teaches self-control and understanding, righteousness and courage; nothing in life is more useful for human beings than these.

target_units.text: Counsel and security are mine; understanding is mine, and strength is mine.
Through me kings reign, and rulers write righteousness.
Through me great men become great, and through me sovereigns rule the earth.
I love those who love me, and those who seek me will find me.
Wealth and glory belong to me, and possession of many things and righteousness.
It is better to reap me than gold and precious stone, and my produce is better than choice silver.
I walk in ways of righteousness, and move in the midst of paths of just judgment,

relationship: close wise understanding of riddles
rationale: Wisdom's understanding of turns of speech and solutions of riddles corresponds to the stated purpose of Proverbs: understanding obscure sayings and wise riddles.
source_text: And if anyone longs for wide experience, she knows ancient things and infers what is to come; she understands turns of speech and solutions of riddles; she knows signs and wonders beforehand, and the outcomes of seasons and times.

target_units.text: and understand a comparison and an obscure saying, the utterances of the wise and riddles.

relationship: parallel wisdom as counselor
rationale: The speaker chooses wisdom as counselor and encouragement; personified Wisdom in Proverbs likewise makes counsel her dwelling and possesses counsel and security.
source_text: Therefore I decided to take her to live with me, knowing that she would be a counselor of good things to me and encouragement amid cares and sorrow.

target_units.text: I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling, and I have called upon knowledge and reflection.
The fear of the Lord hates injustice, insolence and arrogance and the ways of wicked people; and I hate the perverted ways of evil people.
Counsel and security are mine; understanding is mine, and strength is mine.

relationship: parallel honor gained through wisdom
rationale: Wisdom brings the young speaker honor; Proverbs likewise promises that honoring her will bring exaltation and a crown of grace, without the same age contrast.
source_text: Through her I will have glory among the crowds, and, though young, honor among elders.

target_units.text: Fortify her, and she will exalt you; honor her so that she may embrace you,
so that she may give your head a crown of graces and shield you with a crown of delight.

relationship: narrative example of admired wise judgment
rationale: The anticipated keenness in judgment corresponds to Israel's response to Solomon's judgment, recognizing God's discernment within him.
source_text: I will be found keen in judgment and will be admired in the sight of rulers.

target_units.text: All Israel heard this judgment the king had given, and they feared the king, for they saw that God’s discernment was within him to carry out justice.

relationship: close silenced-listeners image
rationale: The speaker expects listeners to wait and place hands on their mouths; Job recalls powerful people stopping speech and putting a finger to their mouths before him.
source_text: When I am silent they will wait for me, and when I speak they will pay attention; if I speak at length, they will place a hand upon their mouth.

target_units.text: Powerful men stopped speaking, placing a finger upon their mouths.
Those who heard called me blessed, and their tongues clung to their throats.

relationship: parallel enduring remembrance of righteousness
rationale: Wisdom promises the speaker everlasting remembrance; the psalm likewise calls the righteous person an everlasting memorial.
source_text: Through her I will have immortality, and will leave an everlasting remembrance to those after me.

target_units.text: For he will never be shaken; the righteous person will be an everlasting memorial.

relationship: parallel governance through wisdom
rationale: The speaker expects to govern peoples through wisdom; Proverbs explicitly declares that kings and sovereigns rule through her.
source_text: I will govern peoples, and nations will be subjected to me.

target_units.text: Through me kings reign, and rulers write righteousness.
Through me great men become great, and through me sovereigns rule the earth.

relationship: parallel peaceful companionship with wisdom
rationale: Life with wisdom brings gladness without bitterness or anguish; Proverbs similarly describes all her paths as peaceful.
source_text: When I enter my house, I will rest beside her; for companionship with her has no bitterness, and life with her no anguish, but gladness and joy.

target_units.text: Her ways are good ways, and all her paths are in peace.

relationship: internal wisdom-incorruption connection
rationale: The speaker finds immortality in kinship with wisdom; the earlier chain joins attention to her laws with incorruption and nearness to God.
source_text: Having reasoned these things within myself and considered in my heart that immortality is in kinship with wisdom,

target_units.text: love is the keeping of her laws, and attention to laws is assurance of incorruption;
and incorruption brings one near to God.

relationship: parallel benefits of loving companionship with wisdom
rationale: The speaker seeks wisdom for delight, understanding and unfailing wealth; Proverbs likewise promises wealth and filled storehouses to those who love her.
source_text: and in friendship with her is good delight, and in the labors of her hands unfailing wealth, and in the shared exercise of companionship with her understanding, and in sharing her words good renown, I went about seeking how to take her to myself.

target_units.text: Wealth and glory belong to me, and possession of many things and righteousness.
It is better to reap me than gold and precious stone, and my produce is better than choice silver.
I walk in ways of righteousness, and move in the midst of paths of just judgment,
so that I may apportion substance to those who love me, and fill their storehouses with good things.

relationship: close wisdom-as-prayed-for-gift parallel
rationale: Recognizing that God must give wisdom leads the speaker to petition Him; James similarly directs the person lacking wisdom to ask God for it.
source_text: But knowing that I could not otherwise gain possession of her unless God gave her— and this too was understanding: to know whose gift it was— I appealed to the Lord and petitioned Him, and said with my whole heart:

target_units.text: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him.

relationship: close creation-by-divine-word motif
rationale: The prayer addresses the God who made all things by His word; the psalm likewise says the heavens were established by His word and creation followed His command.
source_text: “God of the fathers and Lord of mercy, who made all things by Thy word

target_units.text: By the Lord’s word the heavens were established, and by the spirit of His mouth all their power.
He gathers the sea’s waters like a wineskin; He places the deeps in storehouses.
Let all the earth fear the Lord; let all who inhabit the world be shaken before Him.
For He spoke, and they came to be; He commanded, and they were created.

relationship: close human-creation and dominion parallel
rationale: Wisdom describes humanity fashioned to rule God's creatures; Genesis likewise links creation in God's image with rule over earthly living things.
source_text: and by Thy wisdom fashioned the human being, so that he might rule over the creatures made by Thee

target_units.text: And God said, “Let Us make man in Our image and likeness; and let them rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the cattle, all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”
And God made man; in the image of God He made him; male and female He made them.

And God blessed them, saying, “Grow and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, all the cattle, all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”

relationship: parallel righteous administration
rationale: The human vocation to govern in holiness and upright judgment corresponds to the royal prayer for righteous judgment and protection of the poor.
source_text: and administer the world in holiness and righteousness, and render judgment in uprightness of soul,

target_units.text: For Solomon. God, give Thy judgment to the king, and Thy righteousness to the king’s son,
to judge Thy people in righteousness, and Thy poor in justice.
Let the mountains take up peace for Thy people, and the hills in righteousness.
He will judge the poor of the people, and save the children of the needy, and humble the false accuser,

relationship: Solomonic prayer for wisdom parallel
rationale: The request for wisdom beside God's thrones recalls Solomon's request for a discerning heart and God's grant of wisdom for judgment.
source_text: give me wisdom, who sits beside Thy thrones, and do not reject me from among Thy servants.

target_units.text: Give Thy servant a heart to hear and to judge Thy people in righteousness, discerning between good and evil; for who can judge this weighty people of Thine?”
It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this.
The Lord said to him, “Because you have asked this of Me and have not asked for many days for yourself, or wealth, or the lives of your enemies, but have asked for understanding to hear judgment,
behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a discerning and wise heart, so that no one like you has been before you, and no one like you shall arise after you.

relationship: close slave-and-slave-woman formula
rationale: Both prayers address the Lord as His slave and the son of His slave woman, though Wisdom adds frailty and deficient understanding.
source_text: For I am Thy slave and the son of Thy slave woman, a weak and short-lived human being, deficient in understanding judgment and laws.

target_units.text: O Lord, I am Thy slave; I am Thy slave and the son of Thy slave woman. Thou hast torn apart my bonds.

relationship: related insufficiency of merely human wisdom
rationale: Human perfection without God's wisdom counts as nothing here; Paul likewise exposes worldly wisdom's inadequacy before God's wisdom, with his distinct focus on the crucified Christ.
source_text: For even if someone is perfect among the sons of human beings, without the wisdom that comes from Thee, he will be reckoned as nothing.

target_units.text: Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made the world’s wisdom foolish?
For since, in God’s wisdom, the world did not know God through wisdom, God was pleased through the foolishness of the proclamation to save those who believe.
For Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom,
but we proclaim Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,
but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom.
For God’s foolishness is wiser than human beings, and God’s weakness is stronger than human beings.

relationship: Solomonic divine-election parallel
rationale: The speaker says God chose him as king and judge of His people; Chronicles likewise names God's choice of Solomon for the throne and divine sonship.
source_text: Thou didst choose me as king of Thy people and judge of Thy sons and daughters.

target_units.text: From all my sons—for the Lord gave me many sons—He chose Solomon my son to seat him upon the throne of the Lord’s kingdom over Israel.
God said to me, ‘Solomon your son will build My house and My court, for I have chosen him to be My son, and I will be a Father to him,

relationship: Solomonic temple-building commission
rationale: God's command to build the temple corresponds to Chronicles' explicit choice of Solomon to build God's house; the target does not supply the holy-tent comparison.
source_text: Thou didst tell me to build a temple on Thy holy mountain and an altar in the city of Thy dwelling, a likeness of the holy tent that Thou didst prepare beforehand from the beginning.

target_units.text: God said to me, ‘Solomon your son will build My house and My court, for I have chosen him to be My son, and I will be a Father to him,
and I will set his kingdom upright for ever, if he remains strong to observe My commandments and My judgments, as on this day.’

Now, before the whole assembly of the Lord and in the ears of our God, observe and seek all the commandments of the Lord our God, so that you may inherit the good land and pass it on as an inheritance to your sons after you for ever.

And now, Solomon my son, know the God of your fathers, and serve Him with a whole heart and a willing soul; for the Lord examines every heart and knows every thought. If you seek Him, He shall be found by you; but if you forsake Him, He will forsake you utterly.
See, therefore, that the Lord has chosen you to build Him a house as a sanctuary. Be strong and act.”

relationship: close wisdom-present-at-creation parallel
rationale: Wisdom is with God and present at world-making; Proverbs likewise depicts her beside Him during the establishment of heaven and earth.
source_text: With Thee is wisdom, who knows Thy works and was present when Thou didst make the world, who understands what is pleasing in Thine eyes and what is upright in Thy commandments.

target_units.text: When He was preparing heaven, I was present with Him, and when He was marking out His own throne upon winds.
When He was making the clouds above strong, and when He was setting the springs of the world beneath heaven secure,
and was making the foundations of the earth strong,
I was beside Him, fitting things together; I was the one in whom He delighted. Day by day I rejoiced before Him at every time,

relationship: parallel prayer for divinely given wisdom
rationale: The request that God send heavenly wisdom to guide action corresponds to James's instruction to ask God for wisdom.
source_text: Send her out from the holy heavens, and from the throne of Thy glory send her, so that she may labor at my side, and I may know what is pleasing to Thee.

target_units.text: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him.

relationship: parallel wisdom guarding and guiding conduct
rationale: Wisdom promises prudent guidance and protection; Proverbs likewise says wisdom entering the mind brings guarding counsel and rescue from an evil way.
source_text: For she knows and understands all things, and will guide me prudently in my actions and guard me in her glory;

target_units.text: For if wisdom enters your mind and perception seems good to your soul,
good counsel will guard you, and holy thought will keep you,
so that it may rescue you from an evil way and from a man who says nothing trustworthy.

relationship: Solomonic wisdom for righteous judgment
rationale: The speaker expects to judge God's people rightly through wisdom; Solomon likewise asks for discernment to judge the people in righteousness and receives a wise heart.
source_text: and my works will be acceptable, and I will judge Thy people righteously and be worthy of my father’s thrones.

target_units.text: Give Thy servant a heart to hear and to judge Thy people in righteousness, discerning between good and evil; for who can judge this weighty people of Thine?”
It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this.
The Lord said to him, “Because you have asked this of Me and have not asked for many days for yourself, or wealth, or the lives of your enemies, but have asked for understanding to hear judgment,
behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a discerning and wise heart, so that no one like you has been before you, and no one like you shall arise after you.

relationship: close question about knowing God's purpose
rationale: Wisdom asks who can know the Lord's will; Isaiah similarly asks who knew His mind or could instruct Him as counselor.
source_text: For what human being will know God’s purpose? Or who will conceive what the Lord wills?

target_units.text: Who knew the Lord’s mind, and who became His counselor to instruct Him?
With whom did He take counsel, and who instructed Him? Who showed Him judgment, or who showed Him the way of understanding?

relationship: related limitation of unaided human understanding
rationale: Wisdom calls mortal reasoning uncertain; Paul describes the natural person's inability to receive what requires spiritual discernment, a related limitation in a different argument.
source_text: For the reasonings of mortals are uncertain, and our thoughts precarious;

target_units.text: But a natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to such a person, who cannot know them because they are discerned spiritually.

relationship: close bodily-tent and burden imagery
rationale: Wisdom portrays the earthly tent burdening the mind; Paul likewise describes those in the earthly tent groaning under its burden while awaiting life.
source_text: for a corruptible body weighs down a soul, and the earthly tent burdens a mind full of cares.

target_units.text: For we know that if our earthly house, this tent, is dismantled, we have a building from God, a house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens.
For indeed in this we groan, longing to be clothed over with our dwelling from heaven,
if indeed, even after being unclothed, we shall not be found naked.
For indeed we who are in the tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

relationship: related contrast of earthly and heavenly knowledge
rationale: Wisdom contrasts difficult earthly inference with inaccessible heavenly inquiry; Jesus similarly contrasts failure concerning earthly things with difficulty receiving heavenly things.
source_text: With difficulty we infer the things on earth, and find what lies at hand only with labor; but who has traced out the things in heaven?

target_units.text: If I told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?
And no one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.

relationship: close Spirit-given knowledge of God
rationale: God's purpose becomes known through wisdom and the Spirit sent from above; Paul likewise says the Spirit reveals what belongs to God and what He has freely given.
source_text: And who knew Thy purpose, unless Thou didst give wisdom and send Thy Holy Spirit from on high?

target_units.text: But God revealed them to us through the Spirit, for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
For who among human beings knows the things of a person except the person’s spirit within? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.
Now we did not receive the spirit of the world but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things freely given to us by God.

relationship: related salvation through divine wisdom
rationale: Wisdom concludes that people were saved through wisdom; Paul likewise joins God's wisdom to salvation, explicitly identifying Christ as God's wisdom in his own argument.
source_text: And in this way the paths of those on earth were set right, and human beings were taught what pleases Thee, and were saved by wisdom.”

target_units.text: For since, in God’s wisdom, the world did not know God through wisdom, God was pleased through the foolishness of the proclamation to save those who believe.
For Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom,
but we proclaim Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,
but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom.

relationship: creation background of the first-formed father
rationale: The first-formed father recalls the human formed by God from earth; Genesis supplies that creation background but does not itself attribute deliverance from transgression to Wisdom.
source_text: She guarded the first-formed father of the world, who had been created alone, and delivered him from his own transgression;

target_units.text: And God formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

relationship: close original-human dominion parallel
rationale: Wisdom's gift of strength to rule all things corresponds to God's commission that humanity subdue the earth and rule its creatures.
source_text: and she gave him strength to rule over all things.

target_units.text: And God blessed them, saying, “Grow and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, all the cattle, all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”

relationship: Cain narrative allusion
rationale: The angry brother-killer recalls Cain's distress and killing of Abel. Genesis does not narrate Cain's immediate death, so the source's perishing with passions is not treated as an identical narrative detail.
source_text: But an unrighteous man, departing from her in his anger, perished with the passions that made him kill his brother.

target_units.text: but He gave no heed to Cain and his offerings. And Cain was greatly distressed, and his face fell.
And the Lord God said to Cain, “Why are you so distressed, and why has your face fallen?
If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be still. His turning shall be toward you, and you shall rule over him.”
And Cain said to Abel his brother, “Let us go out into the field.” And while they were in the field, Cain rose against Abel his brother and slew him.

relationship: Noah-and-ark narrative allusion
rationale: The righteous man's rescue through humble wood recalls the timber ark and covenant of preservation given to Noah; Wisdom adds her guiding role.
source_text: Because of him the earth was being flooded, but wisdom again saved it, steering the righteous man by means of humble wood.

target_units.text: “Therefore make yourself an ark of squared timber. Make compartments within the ark, and coat it inside and out with pitch.
And this is how you shall make it: the ark shall be three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.
Make the ark taper toward the top, and finish it to a cubit above. Set the door of the ark in its side, and make it with lower, second, and third storeys.
“And behold, I am bringing a flood of water upon the earth, to destroy all flesh beneath heaven in which is the breath of life. Everything upon the earth shall die.
But I will establish My covenant with you. And you shall enter the ark, you and your sons, your wife and your sons’ wives with you.

relationship: Abraham's child-sacrifice test allusion
rationale: The righteous man's strength against compassion for his child corresponds to Abraham's binding of Isaac and refusal to withhold his beloved son; this target addresses that clause, not the earlier confused nations.
source_text: When nations were confounded in their shared wickedness, she recognized the righteous man and kept him blameless before God, and preserved him strong against compassion for his child.

target_units.text: and came to the place of which God had spoken to him. And Abraham built an altar there, and laid the wood upon it, and bound together the feet of Isaac his son, and laid him upon the altar, upon the wood.
And Abraham stretched out his hand to take the knife, to slaughter his son.
And an angel of the Lord called to him out of the heaven, and said to him, “Abraham, Abraham.” And he said, “Behold, here am I.”
And he said, “Do not lay your hand upon the lad or do anything to him; for now I know that you fear God, and have not spared your beloved son for my sake.”

relationship: Lot's rescue from fiery destruction
rationale: The escaping righteous man recalls Lot being brought out before the Lord's fire overthrew the cities.
source_text: When the ungodly were being destroyed, she rescued a righteous man who fled the fire descending upon the Five Cities.

target_units.text: And at dawn, the angels urged Lot, saying, “Arise, take your wife and your two daughters whom you have, and depart, so that you do not perish with the lawless deeds of the city.”
And they were troubled; and the angels took hold of his hand, and the hand of his wife, and the hands of his two daughters, because the Lord spared him.

And when they had brought them outside, they said, “Save your own life. Do not look behind you or stand anywhere in the surrounding country. Escape to the mountain, so that you are not swept away with them.”
And Lot said to them, “I beg you, lord,
for your servant has found mercy before you, and you have shown me your great righteousness by preserving my life. Yet I cannot escape to the mountain, for calamities may overtake me, and I may die.
Behold, this city is near enough for me to flee to, and it is small. There I shall be saved; is it not small? And my soul shall live.”
And he said to him, “Behold, I have regarded your face in this matter also, that I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken.
So hurry and be saved there; for I can do nothing until you enter it.” Therefore he called the name of that city Zoar.
The sun rose upon the earth, and Lot entered into Zoar.
And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of the heaven;
and He overthrew those cities, and all the surrounding country, and all that lived in the cities, and all that sprang from the earth.

relationship: close salt-pillar and smoking-land allusion
rationale: The standing salt pillar and smoking wasteland recall Lot's wife becoming salt and Abraham seeing furnace-like vapor over the destroyed country; Genesis does not mention unripened plants.
source_text: As a witness to its wickedness there still stands a smoking wasteland, and plants whose fruit never reaches ripeness, and a standing pillar of salt, a memorial to a disbelieving soul.

target_units.text: And his wife looked behind her, and became a pillar of salt.
And Abraham rose early in the morning, and went to the place where he had stood before the Lord.
And he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward the land of the surrounding country; and he saw, and behold, a flame rose from the earth as the vapour of a furnace.

relationship: parallel enduring warning from Sodom's destruction
rationale: Wisdom treats the destroyed region as a memorial of folly; Peter likewise calls Sodom and Gomorrah an example for future ungodly people.
source_text: For by passing wisdom by, they were harmed not only by failing to know what is good, but also left life a memorial of their folly, so that even in the things in which they failed they could not escape notice.

target_units.text: and reduced the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes, condemning them to overthrow, having made them an example for those who would live ungodly lives,

relationship: parallel rescue of the godly from trouble
rationale: Wisdom rescues her servants after the Lot example; Peter similarly moves from Lot's rescue to the Lord's ability to rescue godly people from trial.
source_text: But wisdom rescued those who served her from troubles.

target_units.text: and rescued righteous Lot, who was distressed by the lawless people’s conduct in debauchery—
for by what he saw and heard, that righteous man, living among them, tormented his righteous soul day after day over their lawless deeds—
then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment,

relationship: Jacob's guided flight and heavenly revelation
rationale: The fugitive shown divine realities recalls Jacob's dream of the heavenly ladder and God's promise to guard him on every road, after the brother's anger described in Genesis 27.
source_text: She guided a righteous man fleeing his brother’s anger along upright paths; she showed him God’s kingdom and gave him knowledge of holy things; she made him prosper in his hardships and multiplied the fruit of his labors.

target_units.text: And he dreamed, and behold, a ladder was set upon the earth, whose top reached to heaven; and the angels of God ascended and descended upon it.
And the Lord stood firm upon it, and said, “I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac. Do not fear; the land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your seed.

“And your seed shall be as the sand of the earth, and shall spread toward the sea, and toward the south, and toward the north, and toward the east; and in you and in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.
“And behold, I am with you, guarding you on every road wherever you go; and I will bring you back into this land, for I will not forsake you until I have done all that I have spoken to you.”
And Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, “The Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.”
And he was afraid and said, “How fearful is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”

relationship: Jacob protected against exploitation
rationale: Wisdom's protection and enrichment of the exploited righteous man correspond to Jacob's account of Laban's cheating and God's transfer of livestock to him.
source_text: She stood beside him against those who overpowered him in their greed, and made him rich.

target_units.text: “And your father has cheated me, and changed my wages of ten lambs; but God has not allowed him to harm me.
“If he said, ‘The variously marked shall be your wages,’ then all the sheep bore variously marked young; and if he said, ‘The white shall be your wages,’ then all the sheep bore white young.
“And God has taken away all your father’s livestock, and given them to me.
“And when the sheep were mating, I saw them with my eyes in a dream; and behold, the male goats and rams mounting the sheep and goats were white-marked, variously marked, and ash-grey with spots.
“And the angel of God said to me in a dream, ‘Jacob.’ And I said, ‘What is it?’
“And he said, ‘Lift up your eyes and see the male goats and rams mounting the sheep and goats, white-marked, variously marked, and ash-grey with spots; for I have seen all that Laban does to you.

relationship: Jacob's contest and divine preservation
rationale: The mighty contest and discovery of the strength of devotion recall Jacob's wrestling, blessing, new name and declaration that his life was preserved after seeing God.
source_text: She guarded him from enemies and kept him safe from those lying in wait; she presided over a mighty contest for him, so that he might know that devotion to God is stronger than everything.

target_units.text: And Jacob was left alone; and a man wrestled with him until morning.
And he saw that he could not prevail against him, and touched the broad part of his thigh; and the broad part of Jacob’s thigh became numb as he wrestled with him.
And he said to him, “Let me go, for dawn has risen.” And he said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”
And he said to him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Jacob.”
And he said to him, “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, for you have been strong with God, and with men you are mighty.”
And Jacob asked and said, “Tell me your name.” And he said, “Why do you ask my name?” And he blessed him there.
And Jacob called the name of that place Form of God, “For I have seen God face to face, and my life has been preserved.”

relationship: Joseph's refusal of sin
rationale: The sold righteous man rescued from sin recalls Joseph refusing his master's wife's demand because it would be evil before God.
source_text: She did not abandon a righteous man who had been sold, but rescued him from sin;

target_units.text: And after these things his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph, and said, “Lie with me.”
But he would not, and said to his master’s wife, “If my master concerns himself with nothing in his house because of me, and has committed all that he has into my hands,
“and nothing in this house is above me, and nothing has been withheld from me except you, because you are his wife, how shall I do this evil thing, and sin before God?”
And though she spoke to Joseph day after day, he did not listen to her, to sleep with her and have relations with her.
And on a certain day Joseph entered the house to do his work, and none of the household was inside.
And she caught him by his garments, saying, “Lie with me.” And he left his garments in her hands, and fled and went outside.

relationship: Joseph's elevation after imprisonment
rationale: The movement from bonds to authority over rulers culminates in Pharaoh's recognition of Joseph's divine discernment and appointment over Egypt; the surrounding Genesis 39 narrative supplies the false accusation and imprisonment.
source_text: she went down with him into a pit and did not leave him in bonds, until she brought him the scepters of kingship and authority over those who ruled him; she showed those who accused him to be liars and gave him everlasting glory.

target_units.text: And Pharaoh said to all his servants, “Shall we find such a man as this, who has the Spirit of God in him?”
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Since God has shown you all these things, there is no man more prudent and discerning than you.
“You shall be over my house, and all my people shall obey your mouth; only in the throne shall I be above you.”
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Behold, I set you today over all the land of Egypt.”
And Pharaoh took his ring from his hand and put it upon Joseph’s hand, and clothed him in a robe of fine linen, and put a golden collar about his neck.
And he made him ride in his second chariot, and a herald proclaimed before him; and he set him over all the land of Egypt.
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I am Pharaoh; without you no one shall lift up his hand in all the land of Egypt.”

relationship: Israel's liberation from oppression
rationale: Wisdom's rescue of a holy people corresponds to the Lord's promise to free Israel from Egyptian slavery and take them as His people.
source_text: She rescued a holy people and blameless offspring from a nation of oppressors;

target_units.text: Go, say to the sons of Israel: ‘I am the Lord. I will bring you out from the Egyptians’ domination and deliver you from slavery. I will ransom you with an uplifted arm and with great judgment.
And I will take you to Myself for a people, and I will be your God; and you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from the oppression of the Egyptians.

relationship: Moses opposing Pharaoh through signs
rationale: Wisdom's entrance into a servant and opposition to kings through wonders recalls Moses and Aaron's commission to confront Pharaoh with God's multiplied signs.
source_text: she entered the soul of a servant of the Lord and opposed terrifying kings with wonders and signs.

target_units.text: And the Lord said to Moses, “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh; and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet.
You shall speak to him all that I command you; and Aaron your brother shall speak to Pharaoh, that he may let the sons of Israel go out of his land.
I will harden Pharaoh’s heart and multiply My signs and My wonders in the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh will not listen to you. I will lay My hand on Egypt and bring out My people, the sons of Israel, from the land of Egypt with My power and great vengeance.
All the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord when I stretch out My hand over Egypt and bring the sons of Israel out from among them.”
Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded them; so they did.

relationship: close cloud-and-fire guidance allusion
rationale: The covering by day and flame by night correspond to the cloud and fire pillars guiding Israel in Exodus.
source_text: She repaid the holy ones the reward of their labors, guided them on a marvelous way, and became for them a covering by day and a flame of stars by night.

target_units.text: God led them by day in a pillar of cloud to show them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire.
The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not cease before all the people.

relationship: Red Sea crossing allusion
rationale: Wisdom's guidance across the Red Sea corresponds to the opened sea and Israel's passage between walls of water.
source_text: She brought them across the Red Sea and led them through abundant water;

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. The Lord drove the sea back with a violent south wind all night and made the sea dry. The water was split.
The sons of Israel entered the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.

relationship: Egyptian drowning and shore allusion
rationale: The overwhelmed enemies cast up from the depth correspond to the returning sea drowning Egypt's army and Israel seeing their bodies on the shore.
source_text: but their enemies she overwhelmed with the flood and cast them up from the depth of the abyss.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and toward daybreak the water returned to its place. The Egyptians fled beneath the water, and the Lord shook the Egyptians into the midst of the sea.
The water returned and covered the chariots, the riders, and all Pharaoh’s force that had entered the sea after them. Not one of them remained.
But the sons of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.
The Lord rescued Israel that day from the Egyptians’ hand, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.

relationship: song after sea-deliverance allusion
rationale: The united hymn praising God's fighting hand corresponds to Moses and Israel singing of the drowned enemy and the Lord's victorious right hand.
source_text: Therefore the righteous plundered the ungodly and sang hymns, Lord, to Thy holy name, and praised with one accord Thy hand that fought for them;

target_units.text: Then Moses and the sons of Israel sang this song to God, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for He has been gloriously glorified; horse and rider He has cast into the sea.
He has become a helper and a shelter to me for salvation; He is my God, and I will glorify Him; the God of my father, and I will exalt Him.
The Lord shatters wars; the Lord is His name.
Pharaoh’s chariots and his host He has cast into the sea; chosen riders, officers, He has drowned in the Red Sea.
With the sea He covered them; they sank into the deep as a stone.
Thy right hand, O Lord, has been glorified in strength; Thy right hand, O Lord, has shattered enemies.

relationship: close infants' mouths and divine praise motif
rationale: Wisdom enables infants' tongues to speak in the setting of praise; the psalm likewise attributes praise from infants' mouths to God.
source_text: for wisdom opened the mouth of the mute and made the tongues of infants speak clearly.

target_units.text: From the mouth of infants and nursing children Thou didst prepare praise, because of Thine enemies, to bring down the enemy and the avenger.

relationship: parallel mediation through the Exodus prophet
rationale: Wisdom prospers the people's works by a holy prophet; Hosea similarly says the Lord brought Israel from Egypt and preserved him through a prophet.
source_text: She prospered their works by the hand of a holy prophet.

target_units.text: Through a prophet the Lord brought Israel up from Egypt, and through a prophet he was preserved.

relationship: wilderness-journey background
rationale: Travel through an uninhabited, trackless desert corresponds to the Lord's leading through the great, fearful and waterless wilderness.
source_text: They traveled through an uninhabited desert and pitched tents in trackless places;

target_units.text: who led you through that great and fearful wilderness, wherein were biting serpents, and scorpions, and thirst, where there was no water; who brought forth for you a spring of water out of the sheer rock;

relationship: narrative example of repelling desert enemies
rationale: The people's opposition to adversaries corresponds to Israel's battle with Amalek and Joshua's rout of the attackers.
source_text: they opposed their adversaries and repelled their enemies.

target_units.text: Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim.

And Moses said to Joshua, “Choose for yourself able men, and go out and draw up for battle against Amalek tomorrow; and behold, I shall stand upon the summit of the hill, with the staff of God in my hand.”
Joshua did as Moses had told him and went out to take his stand against Amalek. Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
Whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; whenever he lowered his hands, Amalek prevailed.
Moses’ hands were heavy. They took a stone, put it beneath him, and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur steadied his hands, one on each side, so that Moses’ hands remained supported until sunset.
Joshua routed Amalek and all his people with the slaughter of the sword.

relationship: close thirst-and-rock-water allusion
rationale: The thirsty people's appeal and water from rock correspond to the thirst at Rephidim, Moses's cry and the Lord's provision from Horeb's rock.
source_text: They thirsted and called upon Thee, and water was given them from a sheer rock, and a cure for thirst from hard stone.

target_units.text: And the people thirsted there for water, and murmured against Moses, saying, “Why have you brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?”
Moses cried out to the Lord, “What shall I do with this people? A little more, and they will stone me to death!”
And the Lord said to Moses, “Go before this people, and take with you some of the elders of the people; and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the river, and go.
Behold, I stand before you there upon the rock in Horeb; and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come forth from it, and My people shall drink.” And Moses did so before the sons of Israel.

relationship: internal development of one creation serving opposite ends
rationale: The principle of enemies punished while Israel benefits is developed through harmful creatures for oppressors and quail as food for God's people.
source_text: For through the very things by which their enemies were punished, they themselves received benefits in their need.

target_units.text: Therefore they were deservedly punished through similar creatures and tormented by a multitude of beasts.
In contrast to that punishment, Thou didst benefit Thy people: to meet their eager appetite Thou didst prepare quail as food, a novel taste,

so that those, though desiring food, would turn away even from their necessary appetite because of the loathsomeness of the creatures sent upon them, while these, after a brief lack, would share in a novel taste.

relationship: river-turned-to-blood allusion
rationale: The ever-flowing river made bloody corresponds to the Nile water struck into blood, killing fish and becoming undrinkable.
source_text: Instead of the source of an ever-flowing river turbid with bloody gore,

target_units.text: And the Lord said to Moses, “Say to Aaron your brother, ‘Take your staff, and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, and over their canals, and over their marshes, and over all their standing water, and it shall become blood.’” And there was blood throughout all the land of Egypt, both in wood and in stone.
Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded. He raised his staff and struck the river’s water before Pharaoh and his attendants, and all the water in the river turned to blood.
The fish in the river died, and the river stank. The Egyptians could not drink its water, and there was blood throughout the land of Egypt.

relationship: background of the infant-killing decree
rationale: Wisdom interprets the water contrast as a rebuke for killing infants; Exodus supplies Pharaoh's orders to kill Hebrew boys and cast them into the river.
source_text: as a rebuke to the decree for killing infants, Thou didst give them abundant water beyond their expectation,

target_units.text: And he said, “When you attend the Hebrew women in childbirth, and they are about to give birth, if the child is male, kill him; but if the child is female, preserve her.”
But the midwives feared God. They did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them, and they kept the boys alive.
And the king of Egypt called the midwives and said to them, “Why have you done this thing, and kept the male children alive?”
The midwives said to Pharaoh, “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they give birth before the midwives come to them.” And they bore children.
God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied and became very strong.
And because the midwives feared God, they made houses for themselves.
And Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, “Cast every male child born to the Hebrews into the river, but keep every female child alive.”

relationship: internal parallel of need as instruction
rationale: Israel's thirst teaches how opponents were punished; the later food contrast likewise says Israel's brief need showed how their enemies were tormented.
source_text: showing through the thirst of that time how Thou didst punish their opponents.

target_units.text: For unavoidable need had to come upon those who oppressed, but these only had to be shown how their enemies were tormented.

relationship: parallel merciful testing in the wilderness
rationale: Wisdom treats Israel's trials as discipline in mercy; Deuteronomy likewise explains wilderness deprivation as testing and fatherly instruction.
source_text: For when they were tested, although disciplined in mercy, they learned how the ungodly were tormented when judged in wrath.

target_units.text: And you shall remember all the way wherein the Lord your God led you in the wilderness, to afflict you and to test you, that the things in your heart might be known, whether you would keep His commandments or not.

And He afflicted you, and made you hunger, and fed you with manna, which your fathers did not know, that He might declare unto you that man shall not live by bread alone, but man shall live by every word that proceeds through the mouth of God.
Your garments did not wear out upon you, neither did your feet become calloused; behold, these forty years.
And you shall know in your heart that, as a man chastens his son, so shall the Lord your God chasten you.

relationship: parallel fatherly divine discipline
rationale: The source distinguishes a father's instruction of Israel from a condemning king's judgment; Hebrews elaborates the fatherly side through God's beneficial discipline of sons.
source_text: For these Thou didst test as a father giving instruction, but those Thou didst examine as a stern king condemning them.

target_units.text: For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and scourges every son He receives.”
Endure for discipline. God deals with you as sons; for what son is there whom a father does not discipline?
But if you are without discipline, in which all have become partakers, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.
Furthermore, we had our fathers in the flesh to discipline us, and we respected them. But shall we not much more submit to the Father of spirits and live?
For they disciplined us for a few days according to what seemed right to them, but He for our benefit, so that we may share in His holiness.

relationship: internal recognition of God through contrasted rescue
rationale: Enemies recognize the Lord on hearing of benefits given to Israel; the later account similarly says rescue convinced enemies that God delivers from every evil.
source_text: For when they heard that the others had received benefits through their own punishments, they became aware of the Lord.

target_units.text: Through this Thou didst also convince our enemies that Thou art the One who rescues from every evil.

relationship: Moses's final recognition in Egypt
rationale: The once exposed and rejected person later admired corresponds to Moses becoming great in the Egyptians' sight; his infancy is supplied by the separately read Exodus 2 context.
source_text: For the one long ago cast out in exposure, whom they rejected with mockery, they marveled at in the final outcome, having thirsted unlike the righteous.

target_units.text: The Lord gave His people favour in the Egyptians’ sight, and they lent to them. The man Moses became very great in the sight of the Egyptians, Pharaoh, and all his attendants.

relationship: animal-plague narrative background
rationale: The punishment through irrational animals recalls frogs covering Egypt. Wisdom adds its interpretation as recompense for animal worship, which these Exodus verses do not state.
source_text: In return for the senseless reasonings of their unrighteousness, in which they went astray and worshiped irrational creeping things and worthless beasts, Thou didst send upon them a multitude of irrational animals for vengeance,

target_units.text: And the Lord said to Moses, “Say to Aaron your brother, ‘Stretch out the staff in your hand over the rivers, and over the canals, and over the marshes, and bring up the frogs.’”
Aaron stretched out his hand over Egypt’s waters and brought up the frogs. The frogs were brought up and covered the land of Egypt.

relationship: narrative example of punishment matching wrongdoing
rationale: Adoni-bezek explicitly recognizes his own mutilation as God's repayment for the same act he inflicted on others, illustrating Wisdom's matching-recompense principle.
source_text: so that they might know that through the things by which someone sins, through those things he is punished.

target_units.text: Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him, seized him, and cut off the extremities of his hands and his feet.

Adoni-bezek said, “Seventy kings, with the extremities of their hands and feet cut off, used to gather what was beneath my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me.” They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.

relationship: related creation from an unformed condition
rationale: Wisdom appeals to God's creative power over unformed matter; Genesis describes the earth as unseen and unformed before the command for light, without resolving every philosophical implication of Wisdom's wording.
source_text: For Thine all-powerful hand, which created the world from unformed matter, was not at a loss to send upon them a multitude of bears or fierce lions,

target_units.text: In the beginning God made heaven and earth.
Now the earth was unseen and unformed, and darkness was over the deep; and the Spirit of God was moving over the water.
And God said, “Let there be light.” And there was light.

relationship: close measure-and-weight ordering imagery
rationale: God's arrangement by measure, number and weight corresponds to Isaiah's depiction of measured waters, spanned heaven and weighed mountains.
source_text: Even without these, they could have fallen at a single breath, pursued by justice and winnowed away by the breath of Thy power; but Thou didst arrange all things by measure and number and weight.

target_units.text: Who measured the water with His hand, heaven with a span, and all the earth with a handful? Who weighed mountains with a weight and wooded valleys with a balance?

relationship: parallel irresistible divine strength
rationale: Wisdom asks who can oppose God's mighty arm; Job similarly asks who hardened himself against the mighty God and endured.
source_text: For great strength is always at Thy disposal, and who will oppose the might of Thine arm?

target_units.text: For He is wise in understanding, mighty and great. Who grew hard against Him and endured?

relationship: close drop-and-scale comparison
rationale: Wisdom compares the world with a slight tipping of scales and a dew drop; Isaiah likewise compares nations with a bucket's drop and a scale's slight tipping.
source_text: For the whole world before Thee is like a slight tipping of the scales, and like a drop of morning dew that has fallen upon the earth.

target_units.text: If all the nations were counted like a drop from a bucket and like a scale’s slight tipping, they will also be counted like spittle.

relationship: parallel mercy directed toward repentance
rationale: God overlooks sins with repentance in view; Romans likewise says divine kindness and forbearance lead people to repentance.
source_text: But Thou hast mercy on all, because Thou canst do all things, and Thou overlookest human sins with a view to repentance.

target_units.text: Or do you despise the wealth of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?

relationship: parallel kindness toward all God's works
rationale: God loves what He made here; the psalm likewise extends the Lord's kindness and compassion over all His works.
source_text: For Thou lovest all existing things and abhorrest nothing that Thou didst make; for Thou wouldst not have fashioned anything while hating it.

target_units.text: The Lord is kind to all, and His compassions are over all His works.

relationship: parallel creation's dependence on God's sustaining will
rationale: Wisdom asks how anything could endure without God's will; the psalm depicts creatures depending on His food, breath and renewing Spirit.
source_text: How could anything have endured unless Thou didst will it, or what had not been called by Thee have been preserved?

target_units.text: All wait for Thee to give them food at the right time.
When Thou givest to them, they will gather; when Thou openest Thy hand, all things will be filled with goodness.
When Thou turnest Thy face away, they will be troubled. Thou wilt take back their breath, and they will fail and return to their dust.
Thou wilt send Thy Spirit, and they will be created, and Thou wilt renew the face of the earth.

relationship: related divine ownership of the living world
rationale: Wisdom grounds God's sparing care in all things belonging to Him; the psalm likewise declares the earth, its fullness and inhabitants to be the Lord's.
source_text: But Thou sparest all things, because they are Thine, Master who loves life.

target_units.text: A psalm of David, for the first day of the week. The earth and its fullness belong to the Lord, the inhabited world and all who dwell in it.

relationship: internal parallel of the Spirit's universal presence
rationale: The incorruptible Spirit in all things corresponds to the opening declaration that the Lord's Spirit has filled the inhabited world.
source_text: For Thine incorruptible Spirit is in all things.

target_units.text: For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world, and that which holds all things together has knowledge of utterance.

relationship: parallel patient correction for repentance
rationale: Gradual reproof seeks release from evil and renewed belief; Romans similarly presents God's patient kindness as leading to repentance.
source_text: Therefore Thou reprovest those who fall away little by little, and admonishest them by reminding them of the things in which they sin, so that, freed from evil, they may believe in Thee, Lord.

target_units.text: Or do you despise the wealth of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?

relationship: background of the land's former inhabitants
rationale: The introduction of the ancient inhabitants leads into their judgment; Deuteronomy likewise explains the removal of nations from the inherited land through their ungodliness.
source_text: For the ancient inhabitants of Thy holy land,

target_units.text: Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God consumes these nations from before you: Because of my righteous deeds the Lord has brought me in to inherit this good land. Rather, because of the ungodliness of these nations the Lord shall destroy them from before you.

You do not enter to inherit their land for your righteousness, nor for the holiness of your heart; but because of the ungodliness of these nations the Lord shall destroy them from before you, and that He may establish His covenant which He sware unto your fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

relationship: close condemnation of sorcery and forbidden rites
rationale: Wisdom's detestable sorcery and rites correspond to Deuteronomy's prohibited divination, spells and practices that occasion the nations' removal.
source_text: whom Thou didst hate for practicing the most detestable things— works of sorcery and unholy rites,

target_units.text: And when you enter the land which the Lord your God gives you, you shall not learn to do after the abominations of those nations.
There shall not be found among you one who purifies his son or his daughter by fire, or practises divination, or interprets spoken omens, or observes auguries, or works sorcery,
or chants spells, or is a medium, or observes portents, or inquires of the dead.
For everyone who does these things is an abomination unto the Lord your God; for because of these abominations the Lord shall destroy them from before you.

relationship: parallel condemnation of ritual child-killing
rationale: Wisdom condemns murdered children in unholy ritual; the psalm likewise condemns sacrificing sons and daughters and shedding their innocent blood, without describing the flesh-eating detail.
source_text: merciless murders of children, and an entrail-devouring feast of human flesh and blood— initiates from the midst of a ritual company,

target_units.text: They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons,
and shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters whom they sacrificed to Canaan’s carved images; the land was murdered with blood,

relationship: background of destroyed nations and child sacrifice
rationale: Wisdom connects murderous parents with removal by Israel's ancestors; Deuteronomy likewise joins the nations' destruction with the abomination of burning children to their gods.
source_text: and parents who were murderers of helpless lives, Thou didst will to destroy by the hands of our fathers,

target_units.text: And if the Lord your God destroys from before you the nations whither you go to inherit their land, and you inherit their possession and dwell in their land,

take heed unto yourself, that you do not seek to follow them after they have been destroyed from before you. You shall not inquire after their gods, saying: How do these nations serve their gods? I also will do so.
You shall not do so unto the Lord your God; for the abominations which the Lord hated they did unto their gods, for they burn their sons and their daughters with fire unto their gods.

relationship: parallel land-transfer under divine promise
rationale: The land's reception of God's children corresponds to Israel inheriting the nations' land as God establishes the oath to the fathers; Deuteronomy cautions against claiming Israel's own righteousness as the cause.
source_text: so that the land most precious to Thee of all might receive a worthy settlement of God’s children.

target_units.text: You do not enter to inherit their land for your righteousness, nor for the holiness of your heart; but because of the ungodliness of these nations the Lord shall destroy them from before you, and that He may establish His covenant which He sware unto your fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

relationship: close hornets and gradual expulsion allusion
rationale: Both describe hornets preceding Israel and the inhabitants being driven out little by little rather than all at once.
source_text: Yet even these Thou didst spare as human beings, and send hornets as forerunners of Thine army, so that they might destroy them little by little.

target_units.text: And I will send hornets before you, and they shall drive out the Amorites, and Hivites, and Canaanites, and Hittites from before you.
I will not drive them out in one year, lest the land become desolate, and the beasts of the land multiply against you;
little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you increase and inherit the land.

relationship: internal comparison of unused divine means
rationale: The ability to crush enemies by beasts or a stern word recalls the earlier hypothetical destructive creatures and single breath; neither passage claims these imagined beasts were actual plagues.
source_text: Thou wast not unable to give the ungodly into the hands of the righteous in battle, or to crush them all at once with terrifying beasts or a stern word;

target_units.text: For Thine all-powerful hand, which created the world from unformed matter, was not at a loss to send upon them a multitude of bears or fierce lions,
or newly created, unknown beasts full of fury, either breathing a fire-breathing blast, or scattering a stench of smoke, or flashing dreadful sparks from their eyes,
whose injury could not only utterly crush them, but whose very appearance could terrify and destroy them.
Even without these, they could have fallen at a single breath, pursued by justice and winnowed away by the breath of Thy power; but Thou didst arrange all things by measure and number and weight.

relationship: parallel delayed judgment as room for repentance
rationale: Gradual judgment gives time to repent despite ingrained evil; Romans similarly contrasts repentance under divine patience with an unrepentant heart storing up wrath.
source_text: but judging them little by little, Thou didst give room for repentance, not unaware that their origin was wicked, and their evil ingrained, and that their reasoning would never change.

target_units.text: Or do you despise the wealth of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?
But by your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment,

relationship: close unanswerable-question formula
rationale: Both ask who could challenge God with the question, 'What hast Thou done?' when His action cannot be turned back.
source_text: For who will say, ‘What hast Thou done?’ Or who will oppose Thy judgment? Who will accuse Thee concerning destroyed nations that Thou didst make? Or who will come to confront Thee as an avenger concerning unrighteous human beings?

target_units.text: If He takes away, who will turn Him back? Who will say to Him, ‘What hast Thou done?’

relationship: parallel exclusive divine authority
rationale: Wisdom denies any rival god to whom the Lord must justify judgment; Deuteronomy likewise declares that no god stands beside Him and none can deliver from His hands.
source_text: For there is no god besides Thee, who cares for all, so that Thou shouldst have to show that Thou hast not judged unjustly;

target_units.text: See, see that I am, and there is no god beside Me. I will put to death, and make alive; I will smite, and I will heal; and there is none that shall deliver out of My hands.

relationship: parallel impotence of rulers before divine judgment
rationale: No king can confront God over His punishment here; the psalm likewise portrays assembled rulers facing divine laughter and anger.
source_text: nor will a king or ruler be able to face Thee concerning those Thou didst punish.

target_units.text: The kings of the earth stood ready, and the rulers gathered together, against the Lord and against His anointed. Diapsalma.
“Let us tear apart their bonds and cast their yoke away from us.”
The One dwelling in heaven will laugh at them, and the Lord will sneer at them.
Then He will speak to them in His anger and trouble them in His fury:

relationship: close appeal to the justice of the universal Judge
rationale: Wisdom rejects condemning one undeserving of punishment; Abraham likewise appeals to the Judge of all earth not to destroy righteous and ungodly indiscriminately.
source_text: But being righteous, Thou administerest all things righteously, regarding it as alien to Thy power to condemn anyone who does not deserve punishment.

target_units.text: And Abraham drew near and said, “Wilt Thou destroy the righteous with the ungodly, and shall the righteous be as the ungodly?
If there are fifty righteous in the city, wilt Thou destroy them? Wilt Thou not spare the whole place for the sake of the fifty righteous, if they are there?
By no means shalt Thou do such a thing, to kill the righteous with the ungodly, so that the righteous shall be as the ungodly. By no means! Thou who judgest all the earth, wilt Thou not do justice?”

relationship: internal connection of power and mercy
rationale: Wisdom derives sparing mercy from universal mastery; the earlier prayer similarly grounds mercy toward all in God's ability to do all things.
source_text: For Thy strength is the beginning of righteousness, and Thy mastery over all makes Thee spare all.

target_units.text: But Thou hast mercy on all, because Thou canst do all things, and Thou overlookest human sins with a view to repentance.

relationship: narrative example of power displayed against defiance
rationale: God displays strength when His power is disbelieved; Exodus likewise interprets Pharaoh's preservation as an occasion to display God's strength amid continued refusal.
source_text: For Thou displayest strength when the completeness of Thy power is disbelieved, and among those who know, Thou exposest their audacity.

target_units.text: For at this time I will send all My blows upon your heart, and upon your attendants and your people, that you may know that there is none other like Me in all the earth.
For now I will stretch out My hand and strike you and your people with death, and you shall be blotted out from the earth.
And for this reason you were preserved, that I might show My strength in you, and that My name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.
Do you still act against My people, refusing to let them go?

relationship: parallel patient and merciful divine governance
rationale: God judges gently with great forbearance; the psalm similarly describes Him as compassionate, merciful and long-suffering.
