source_text: But Thou, master of strength, judgest with gentleness and governest us with great forbearance; for the ability to act is at Thy disposal whenever Thou wilt.

target_units.text: And Thou, Lord God, art compassionate and merciful, long-suffering, abundant in mercy, and true.

relationship: parallel divine mercy as a human ethical example
rationale: God's works teach the righteous to love humanity; Jesus likewise grounds love for enemies and human mercy in the Father's kindness and mercy.
source_text: Through such works Thou didst teach Thy people that the righteous person must love humanity, and make Thy sons hopeful, because Thou givest repentance for sins.

target_units.text: But love your enemies, do good, and lend, expecting nothing back. Your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, because He is kind to the ungrateful and evil.
Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.

relationship: parallel leniency offering release from evil
rationale: Wisdom says even enemies receive time and room to abandon evil; Romans likewise interprets divine patience as an invitation to repentance.
source_text: For if Thou didst punish the enemies of Thy children, who were liable to death, with such attention and leniency, giving times and room through which they might be freed from evil,

target_units.text: Or do you despise the wealth of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?

relationship: background of good promises sworn to the fathers
rationale: The special care for descendants of oath-receiving fathers recalls God's oath to Abraham promising multiplied offspring and blessing.
source_text: with how much care didst Thou judge Thy sons, to whose fathers Thou didst give oaths and covenants of good promises?

target_units.text: saying, “By Myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing, and have not spared your beloved son for My sake,
surely I will bless you, and greatly multiply your seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand upon the shore of the sea; and your seed shall inherit the cities of their adversaries.
And in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have listened to My voice.”

relationship: parallel merciful judgment modeled on God
rationale: Wisdom's discipline teaches people to consider goodness when judging and expect mercy when judged; Luke similarly connects the Father's mercy with human restraint in judgment and reciprocal measure.
source_text: Therefore, while disciplining us, Thou scourgest our enemies with myriad blows, so that when judging we may consider Thy goodness, and when judged we may expect mercy.

target_units.text: Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.
Do not judge, and you will certainly not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will certainly not be condemned. Release, and you will be released.
Give, and it will be given to you. They will put into your lap a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, overflowing; for by the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you.”

relationship: internal recurrence of punishment through one's abominations
rationale: The ungodly are tormented through their own abominations, restating the earlier animal-worship contrast and principle that the instruments of sin become instruments of punishment.
source_text: Therefore those who lived unrighteously in a foolish way of life Thou didst also torment through their own abominations.

target_units.text: In return for the senseless reasonings of their unrighteousness, in which they went astray and worshiped irrational creeping things and worthless beasts, Thou didst send upon them a multitude of irrational animals for vengeance,
so that they might know that through the things by which someone sins, through those things he is punished.

relationship: close foolish exchange for animal images
rationale: Wisdom depicts people mistaking despised animals for gods; Romans likewise describes claimed wisdom becoming folly through exchanging divine glory for animal images.
source_text: For they wandered even farther than the paths of error, supposing that creatures despised even among shameful animals were gods, deceived like senseless infants.

target_units.text: Claiming to be wise, they became foolish,
and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible humanity, and of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things.

relationship: parallel rejected patience followed by judgment
rationale: Failure to heed lighter reproof leads to full divine judgment; Romans similarly contrasts patient kindness with accumulated wrath for unrepentance.
source_text: But those who were not admonished by playful reproofs will experience a judgment worthy of God.

target_units.text: Or do you despise the wealth of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?
But by your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment,

relationship: narrative analogue for recognizing God through creatures
rationale: Wisdom interprets animal punishment as exposing false gods; Exodus depicts failed attempts to produce gnats followed by the magicians' recognition of God's finger, without all of Wisdom's interpretation.
source_text: For as they suffered punishment through the very creatures they had supposed to be gods, they grew indignant at them, and saw and recognized as the true God the One they had long refused to know; therefore the final condemnation also came upon them.

target_units.text: The enchanters tried by their sorceries to bring forth gnats, but they could not. The gnats were on people and four-footed animals.
The enchanters said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God.” But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said.

relationship: close failure to know God from created works
rationale: Both fault people who fail to give God proper recognition despite the evidence of what He made.
source_text: For all human beings in whom ignorance of God was present were futile by nature; from the good things seen they could not know the One who is, nor, attending to the works, did they recognize the Artisan.

target_units.text: because what is known of God is plain among them, for God made it plain to them.
For His invisible qualities, both His eternal power and divinity, have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, understood through the things made, so that they are without excuse,
because, although they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their senseless heart was darkened.

relationship: parallel rejection of worshiping heavenly creation
rationale: Wisdom lists natural powers and heavenly lights falsely treated as gods; Deuteronomy expressly warns against worshiping sun, moon, stars and heaven's array.
source_text: Instead, they supposed fire or wind or swift-moving air, or the circuit of stars or violent water, or the lights of heaven to be gods, rulers of the world.

target_units.text: And lest you lift up your eyes unto heaven, and see the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and all the adornment of heaven, and be led astray to bow down unto them and serve them, which the Lord your God has allotted unto all the nations under heaven.

relationship: related Creator's superiority to the heavens
rationale: Wisdom directs admiration beyond beautiful created things to their Maker; Isaiah likewise challenges comparisons with God and points to His authorship of the heavenly array.
source_text: If, delighted by their beauty, they supposed these things to be gods, let them know how much better than these their Master is; for the Originator of beauty created them.

target_units.text: “Now then, to whom did you liken Me, and shall I be exalted?” said the Holy One.
Lift your eyes on high and see: Who displayed all these? He brings out His array by number and will call all by name. From abundant glory and in strength’s might, nothing escaped you.

relationship: parallel inference from cosmic power to its Maker
rationale: The power of created things should direct thought to their stronger Maker; Isaiah similarly attributes the ordered heavenly host to God's abundant might.
source_text: And if they were astonished at their power and activity, let them understand from these how much more powerful the One who fashioned them is.

target_units.text: Lift your eyes on high and see: Who displayed all these? He brings out His array by number and will call all by name. From abundant glory and in strength’s might, nothing escaped you.

relationship: close knowledge of the unseen Maker through visible works
rationale: Wisdom says the Maker is seen by analogy from created greatness and beauty; Romans likewise says invisible divine qualities are understood through created things.
source_text: For from the greatness and beauty of created things their Maker is seen by analogy.

target_units.text: For His invisible qualities, both His eternal power and divinity, have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, understood through the things made, so that they are without excuse,

relationship: related searching for God
rationale: Wisdom grants that some mistaken people are seeking God; Acts likewise describes humanity seeking and feeling its way toward Him, without making the same judgment about their degree of blame.
source_text: Yet the blame upon these is small, for perhaps they themselves go astray while seeking God and wishing to find Him.

target_units.text: so that they might seek God, if perhaps they might feel their way toward Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us.

relationship: parallel attention to creation displacing its Creator
rationale: The attractive appearance of God's works persuades people wrongly; Romans likewise criticizes reverence directed to creation instead of its Creator.
source_text: For living among His works, they search them out and are persuaded by their appearance, because the things seen are beautiful.

target_units.text: who exchanged the truth of God for the lie, and revered and worshiped the creation instead of the Creator, who is blessed throughout the ages. Amen.

relationship: close denial of excuse
rationale: Both explicitly deny excuse to those who fail to recognize God in the setting of available evidence from creation.
source_text: But again, even they are not excusable;

target_units.text: For His invisible qualities, both His eternal power and divinity, have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, understood through the things made, so that they are without excuse,

relationship: parallel accountability for misused available knowledge
rationale: Wisdom questions extensive inquiry that misses the world's Master; Romans likewise treats available knowledge as grounds for accountability when God is not honored.
source_text: for if they were able to know so much that they could investigate the world, how did they not more quickly find the Master of these things?

target_units.text: because what is known of God is plain among them, for God made it plain to them.
For His invisible qualities, both His eternal power and divinity, have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, understood through the things made, so that they are without excuse,
because, although they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their senseless heart was darkened.

relationship: close handmade-metal-idol description
rationale: Both identify the nations' supposed gods as silver or gold and works of human hands.
source_text: But wretched are those whose hopes rest in dead things, who called the works of human hands gods: gold and silver, exercises of craftsmanship, likenesses of living creatures, or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand.

target_units.text: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, works of human hands.

relationship: parallel account of worked wood before idolatry
rationale: Both describe a craftsman's selecting and shaping wood within an argument that contrasts its ordinary human uses with its manufacture into a supposed god.
source_text: Suppose a woodcutting craftsman sawed down a manageable tree, skillfully scraped off all its bark, and, working it handsomely, fashioned a useful vessel for the service of life,

target_units.text: wood, a craftsman set it by measure and arranged it with glue. He made it like a man’s form and human beauty, to set it in a house.
The wood he cut from the woodland was what the Lord planted and rain made grow,
so that it might serve people for burning. Taking some, he warmed himself; after burning it they baked loaves over the pieces. They worked the rest into gods and worship them.

relationship: close wood-scraps cooking motif
rationale: The craftsman burns leftover wood and eats his fill; Isaiah likewise describes using part of the wood to bake bread, roast meat and become satisfied.
source_text: and burned the scraps from the work to prepare food and ate his fill,

target_units.text: Half of it they burned in fire, and after burning it they baked loaves over the pieces. Over it he roasted meat, ate, and was satisfied. Warmed, he said, ‘It is pleasant for me, for I am warm and have seen fire!’

relationship: close leftover-wood idol motif
rationale: Both portray the remainder of useful or burned wood being fashioned into a humanly made god.
source_text: then took the scrap left from these, useful for nothing, a crooked piece of wood grown full of knots, and carved it with the care of his leisure, shaped it with practiced understanding, and made it resemble a human image,

target_units.text: He made the rest into a carved god and worships it and prays, saying, ‘Rescue me, for you are my god.’

relationship: internal recurrence of attractively painted idols
rationale: The image's applied red color and concealed blemishes correspond to the later colored, painted form that stirs foolish desire despite being lifeless.
source_text: or made it like some worthless animal, coating it with red ocher and reddening its surface with paint, and covering every blemish in it,

target_units.text: For neither the evil-devising invention of human beings misled us, nor the fruitless labor of painters, a form stained with varied colors,
the sight of which stirs desire in fools, and one longs for the breathless form of a dead image.

relationship: close fastening an idol to prevent movement
rationale: The image is set in a wall and secured with iron; Jeremiah likewise describes idols fastened with hammers and nails so they do not move.
source_text: and made for it a dwelling worthy of it, set it in a wall, and secured it with iron.

target_units.text: They are adorned with silver and gold; with hammers and nails they fastened them, and they will not move.

relationship: parallel dependence and helplessness of idols
rationale: The maker must stop his image falling because it cannot help itself; Jeremiah similarly presents fastened images that must be carried and cannot provide good.
source_text: He took care that it would not fall, knowing that it cannot help itself; for it is an image and needs help.

target_units.text: They are adorned with silver and gold; with hammers and nails they fastened them, and they will not move.
They must be lifted and carried, because they will not take a step. Do not fear them, because they certainly will not do evil, and no good is in them.

relationship: close petition to a self-made god
rationale: The maker addresses a lifeless image for personal welfare; Isaiah likewise depicts the craftsman praying for rescue to the remainder he made into a god.
source_text: Yet when praying concerning his possessions, marriage, and children, he is not ashamed to address what has no soul; for health he calls upon what is weak,

target_units.text: He made the rest into a carved god and worships it and prays, saying, ‘Rescue me, for you are my god.’

relationship: parallel inability of an idol to supply living action
rationale: Wisdom mocks petitions for life and travel to a dead, immobile object; the psalm likewise lists idols' unusable senses and feet that do not walk.
source_text: for life he petitions what is dead, for assistance he begs what is utterly inexperienced, for a journey what cannot even use its feet,

target_units.text: They have a mouth and will not speak; they have eyes and will not see.
They have ears and will not hear; they have noses and will not smell.
They have hands and will not feel; feet, and will not walk; they will not sound with their throat.

relationship: parallel useless objects asked to provide benefit
rationale: Wisdom exposes the powerless idol asked for successful work; Isaiah likewise calls manufactured gods useless and unable to help their makers.
source_text: and for gain, work, and success of his hands, he asks vigor of what is most powerless with its hands.

target_units.text: All who fashion and carve are futile, making what pleases them, things that will not help them. But they will be ashamed—
all who fashion a god and carve useless things,

relationship: contrast in maritime trust
rationale: Wisdom mocks a sailor's appeal to rotten wood; the psalm instead portrays endangered sailors calling to the Lord, who quiets the waves and guides them to harbor.
source_text: Again, someone preparing for a voyage and about to traverse wild waves calls upon a piece of wood more rotten than the ship carrying him.

target_units.text: Those going down into the sea in ships, doing work on many waters,
they saw the Lord’s works and His wonders in the depth.
He spoke, and a storm wind stood, and its waves were raised.
They rise as far as the heavens and descend as far as the deeps; their soul melted in evils.
They were troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.
They cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and He brought them out of their distresses,
and commanded the storm, and it settled into a breeze, and its waves fell silent.
They rejoiced because they became quiet, and He guided them to the harbor of their desire.

relationship: internal recurrence of wisdom as artisan
rationale: The ship is fashioned through wisdom the artisan; the earlier passage likewise calls wisdom the artisan of all things.
source_text: For the desire for gain devised that ship, and wisdom, the artisan, fashioned it;

target_units.text: I learned all that is hidden and manifest, for wisdom, the artisan of all things, taught me.

relationship: close path-through-the-sea formula
rationale: God's providence provides a way in the sea and safe path among waves, closely recalling Isaiah's description of the Lord making a path in strong water.
source_text: but Thy providence, Father, steers it, for Thou didst give a way even in the sea and a safe path among the waves,

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord, who gives a way in the sea and a path in strong water,

relationship: parallel divine rescue from maritime danger
rationale: Wisdom celebrates salvation even when the traveler lacks skill; the psalm likewise makes rescue depend on the Lord's response and guidance when sailors' wisdom has failed.
source_text: showing that Thou canst save from every danger, so that even someone without skill may embark.

target_units.text: They cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and He brought them out of their distresses,
and commanded the storm, and it settled into a breeze, and its waves fell silent.
They rejoiced because they became quiet, and He guided them to the harbor of their desire.

relationship: ark background for preservation through wood
rationale: The argument about life entrusted to wood leads directly to the flood example; Genesis narrates the floating ark and the preservation of Noah and its occupants amid destruction.
source_text: Thou wilt that the works of Thy wisdom should not be idle; therefore human beings entrust their lives even to a very small piece of wood, and, crossing the surge on a raft, they were brought safely through.

target_units.text: And the waters prevailed and increased greatly upon the earth, and the ark floated upon the waters.
And the waters prevailed exceedingly upon the earth, and covered all the high mountains beneath heaven.
The waters rose fifteen cubits above them and covered all the high mountains.
And all flesh that moved upon the earth died: birds, cattle, wild beasts, every creeping thing that moves upon the earth, and all mankind.
Everything that had the breath of life, everything upon the dry land, died.

And He blotted out every living thing upon the face of the whole earth: mankind, cattle, creeping things, and the birds of heaven. They were blotted out from the earth, and only Noah remained, and those with him in the ark.

relationship: Noah's preservation as hope for continued life
rationale: Wisdom's surviving seed on a raft recalls Noah and the ark's occupants remaining after the flood; the giants belong to the separately read Genesis 6 setting.
source_text: For even at the beginning, when arrogant giants were perishing, the hope of the world took refuge on a raft and left to the age a seed for generation, steered by Thy hand.

target_units.text: And He blotted out every living thing upon the face of the whole earth: mankind, cattle, creeping things, and the birds of heaven. They were blotted out from the earth, and only Noah remained, and those with him in the ark.

relationship: ark-context explanation of blessed wood
rationale: The blessed wood follows the flood rescue and corresponds to Noah's commanded timber ark and promised preservation; this link does not assert an explicit reference to the cross.
source_text: For blessed is wood through which righteousness comes about;

target_units.text: “Therefore make yourself an ark of squared timber. Make compartments within the ark, and coat it inside and out with pitch.
And this is how you shall make it: the ark shall be three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.
Make the ark taper toward the top, and finish it to a cubit above. Set the door of the ark in its side, and make it with lower, second, and third storeys.
“And behold, I am bringing a flood of water upon the earth, to destroy all flesh beneath heaven in which is the breath of life. Everything upon the earth shall die.
But I will establish My covenant with you. And you shall enter the ark, you and your sons, your wife and your sons’ wives with you.

relationship: parallel condemnation of fabricated idols and attachment to them
rationale: Wisdom condemns the handmade god and maker; Deuteronomy calls the carved image an abomination and warns that its possessor can become subject to its ban.
source_text: but the handmade object is accursed, both it and its maker: the one because he made it, and the other because, though corruptible, it was named a god.

target_units.text: You shall burn the graven images of their gods with fire. You shall not covet the silver or gold upon them, nor take it unto yourself, lest you stumble thereby; for it is an abomination unto the Lord your God.
And you shall not bring an abomination into your house, lest you become a thing under the ban, like unto it. You shall utterly reject it, and utterly abhor it, for it is a thing under the ban.

relationship: parallel divine rejection of wickedness and its practitioners
rationale: Wisdom joins God's hatred of ungodliness and the ungodly person; the psalm likewise says God hates workers of lawlessness and abhors the deceitful, bloodthirsty person.
source_text: For equally hateful to God are the ungodly person and his ungodliness;

target_units.text: The lawless will not remain before Thine eyes; Thou didst hate all who work lawlessness.
Thou wilt destroy all who speak falsehood; the Lord abhors a man of bloodshed and deceit.

relationship: parallel joined judgment of idol and human participant
rationale: The deed and doer receive punishment together; Deuteronomy similarly warns that bringing an abominable image home can bring its ban upon the person.
source_text: for what was done will be punished together with the one who did it.

target_units.text: And you shall not bring an abomination into your house, lest you become a thing under the ban, like unto it. You shall utterly reject it, and utterly abhor it, for it is a thing under the ban.

relationship: close idol-as-stumbling-block image
rationale: Wisdom calls idols stumbling blocks and snares for souls; the psalm likewise says service to carved images became a stumbling block.
source_text: Therefore there will also be a visitation upon the nations’ idols, because within God’s creation they became an abomination, stumbling blocks to human souls, and a snare for the feet of fools.

target_units.text: They served their carved images, and it became a stumbling block to them.

relationship: parallel idolatry leading to sexual impurity
rationale: Wisdom connects invented idols with sexual immorality; Romans likewise moves from exchanged divine glory to bodily impurity in disordered desires.
source_text: For the devising of idols is the beginning of sexual immorality, and their invention the corruption of life.

target_units.text: and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible humanity, and of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things.
Therefore God handed them over, in the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that their bodies would be dishonored among them,

relationship: parallel impermanence of false gods
rationale: Wisdom denies that idols will endure forever; Jeremiah similarly calls for gods that did not create heaven and earth to perish.
source_text: For they did not exist from the beginning, nor will they exist for ever;

target_units.text: This is what you will say to them: Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish from the earth and from beneath this heaven.

relationship: parallel end appointed for fabricated gods
rationale: The idols' vainglorious invention is assigned an end; Jeremiah likewise calls fabricated images false and destined to perish at visitation.
source_text: through human vainglory they entered the world, and therefore a swift end was planned for them.

target_units.text: Every human became foolish, without knowledge; every goldsmith was put to shame at his carved things, because they cast false things; there is no spirit in them.
They are futile, mocked works; at the time of their visitation they will perish.

relationship: narrative example of ruler-commanded image worship
rationale: Wisdom describes carved images worshiped by royal command; Daniel supplies a concrete case of commanded worship, without identifying the golden image as a portrait of the king.
source_text: And carved images were worshiped at rulers’ commands; when people could not honor them face to face because they lived far away, they reproduced their distant appearance and made a visible image of the honored king, so that by their zeal they might flatter the absent one as though present.

target_units.text: The herald proclaimed to the crowds, “You are commanded, nations and countries, peoples and languages:
when you hear the sound of trumpet, panpipe, kithara, sambuca, psaltery, symphonia, and every kind of musical instrument, fall down and bow to the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up.
They will throw into the blazing furnace anyone who does not fall down and bow.”

At that time, when all the nations heard the sound of the trumpet and every musical sound, all the nations, tribes, and languages fell down and bowed to the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up before him.

relationship: related artistic production of ideal human beauty
rationale: Wisdom describes a likeness made more beautiful by artistic effort; Isaiah likewise describes an idol made in human form and beauty, without the same royal-flattery motive.
source_text: for, perhaps wishing to please the ruler, he used his art to force the likeness toward greater beauty.

target_units.text: wood, a craftsman set it by measure and arranged it with glue. He made it like a man’s form and human beauty, to set it in a house.

relationship: parallel human likeness promoted to worship
rationale: Wisdom describes a previously honored human becoming an object of worship; Romans likewise condemns replacing divine glory with a corruptible human image.
source_text: The multitude, drawn by the charm of the workmanship, now reckoned as an object of worship the human being whom they had honored a little before.

target_units.text: and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible humanity, and of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things.

relationship: parallel exclusivity of the divine name and honor
rationale: Wisdom condemns giving wood and stone the unshared name; Isaiah likewise declares the Lord's name and refusal to give His glory or praiseworthy deeds to carved images.
source_text: And this became an ambush for life, because human beings, enslaved either to misfortune or to royal power, bestowed upon stones and pieces of wood the name that cannot be shared.

target_units.text: I am the Lord God; this is My name. I will not give My glory to another or My praiseworthy deeds to carved images.

relationship: parallel false declaration of peace amid evil
rationale: Wisdom criticizes calling grave evils peace; Jeremiah similarly exposes dishonest people who proclaim peace while treating the people's fracture with contempt.
source_text: Then it was not enough to go astray about the knowledge of God; living in the great war of ignorance, they also call such great evils peace.

target_units.text: For from their small to their great, all have carried out lawless deeds; from priest to false prophet, all have done false things.
And they treated My people’s fracture with contempt, saying, ‘Peace, peace’; and where is peace?

They were put to shame because they failed, and even so they were not at all ashamed and did not recognize their dishonor. Therefore they will fall in their fall, and at the time of their visitation they will perish, said the Lord.

relationship: parallel condemnation of child-killing rites
rationale: Wisdom condemns rites that murder children; Deuteronomy likewise calls burning children to gods an abomination the Lord hates.
source_text: For while celebrating rites that murder children, or secret mysteries, or frenzied revelries with strange customs,

target_units.text: You shall not do so unto the Lord your God; for the abominations which the Lord hated they did unto their gods, for they burn their sons and their daughters with fire unto their gods.

relationship: parallel collapse of life and marital fidelity
rationale: Wisdom pairs murder with adultery amid ignorance of God; Hosea likewise joins lack of divine recognition with murder, adultery and bloodshed.
source_text: they no longer keep either lives or marriages pure; one kills another by ambush or grieves him by adultery.

target_units.text: Hear the Lord’s word, sons of Israel, for the Lord has a case against the land’s inhabitants: there is no truth, no mercy and no recognition of God upon the land.
Cursing, falsehood, murder, theft and adultery have poured over the land, and they mix bloodshed with bloodshed.

relationship: close catalogue of violence, theft and deception
rationale: The disorderly catalogue of murder, theft and deceit corresponds to Hosea's linked cursing, falsehood, murder, theft and adultery.
source_text: Bloodshed and murder, theft and deceit, hold everything in confusion, corruption, unfaithfulness, disturbance, perjury,

target_units.text: Cursing, falsehood, murder, theft and adultery have poured over the land, and they mix bloodshed with bloodshed.

relationship: related catalogue of moral and relational disorder
rationale: Both accounts connect rejected knowledge of God with disturbed relations, dishonor, faithlessness and broader moral disorder; their lists are not identical.
source_text: confusion of good things, forgetfulness of favor, defilement of souls, alteration of natural relations, disorder in marriages, adultery, and licentiousness.

target_units.text: For this reason God handed them over to dishonorable passions; for their females exchanged natural relations for those contrary to nature,

and likewise the males, leaving natural relations with the female, burned in their desire for one another, males with males committing what is shameful and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.
And just as they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, God handed them over to an unfit mind, to do what is not fitting:
filled with all unrighteousness, wickedness, greed, evil; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malice; whisperers,
slanderers, haters of God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents,
without understanding, faithless, without natural affection, merciless;

relationship: parallel connection of idolatry with proliferating wrongdoing
rationale: Wisdom calls idol worship the source of evil; Romans similarly develops a sequence from exchanged worship to impurity and numerous injustices.
source_text: For worship of nameless idols is the beginning, cause, and end of every evil.

target_units.text: and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible humanity, and of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things.
Therefore God handed them over, in the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that their bodies would be dishonored among them,
who exchanged the truth of God for the lie, and revered and worshiped the creation instead of the Creator, who is blessed throughout the ages. Amen.
