relationship: related accountability for false oaths
rationale: Among the corrupt practices Wisdom names is ready false swearing; Zechariah expressly depicts judgment entering the false swearer's house.
source_text: For they either go mad in their merrymaking, or prophesy lies, or live unjustly, or readily swear falsely.

target_units.text: He said to me, “This is the curse going out over the whole earth, because every thief will be punished by this with death, and every false swearer will be punished by this with death.

I will bring it out, says the Lord Almighty. It will enter the thief’s house and the house of whoever swears falsely by My name; it will lodge within his house and destroy it completely, its timbers and its stones.”

relationship: related swearing by non-gods
rationale: Wisdom exposes people who trust lifeless idols when swearing wrongly; Jeremiah likewise condemns swearing by those who are not gods.
source_text: For trusting in lifeless idols, they do not expect to be harmed when they swear wrongly.

target_units.text: For which of these things should I be merciful to you? Your sons abandoned Me and swore by those who are not gods. And I fed them fully, and they committed adultery and lodged in prostitutes’ houses.

relationship: parallel judgment pursuing false swearing
rationale: Wisdom promises consequences for deceitful oaths despite the idols' helplessness; Zechariah likewise sends divine judgment into the false swearer's house.
source_text: But just consequences will pursue them for both things: because they thought wrongly about God by attending to idols, and swore unjustly in deceit, despising holiness.

target_units.text: He said to me, “This is the curse going out over the whole earth, because every thief will be punished by this with death, and every false swearer will be punished by this with death.

I will bring it out, says the Lord Almighty. It will enter the thief’s house and the house of whoever swears falsely by My name; it will lodge within his house and destroy it completely, its timbers and its stones.”

relationship: parallel divine justice behind oath judgment
rationale: Wisdom locates punishment in justice rather than the power of the named idols; Zechariah explicitly makes the Lord the sender of judgment against false swearing.
source_text: For it is not the power of those by whom they swear, but the justice due to sinners, that always pursues the transgression of the unrighteous.

target_units.text: I will bring it out, says the Lord Almighty. It will enter the thief’s house and the house of whoever swears falsely by My name; it will lodge within his house and destroy it completely, its timbers and its stones.”

relationship: close description of God's patient mercy
rationale: Both address God as patient, merciful and true, grounding trust in His character.
source_text: But Thou, our God, art good and true, patient, and governing all things in mercy.

target_units.text: And Thou, Lord God, art compassionate and merciful, long-suffering, abundant in mercy, and true.

relationship: related rejection of sin as a response to grace
rationale: Wisdom's acknowledgment of belonging to God even amid sin does not endorse continued sin; Paul likewise rejects continuing in sin so that grace may increase.
source_text: For even if we sin, we are Thine, knowing Thy might; but we will not sin, knowing that we have been reckoned as Thine.

target_units.text: What, then, shall we say? Should we remain in sin so that grace may increase?
May it never be! We who died to sin, how will we still live in it?

relationship: close knowledge-of-God and eternal-life association
rationale: Wisdom calls knowledge of God the root of immortality; Jesus likewise describes eternal life in terms of knowing the true God and the One He sent.
source_text: For to know Thee is complete righteousness, and to know Thy might is the root of immortality.

target_units.text: And this is eternal life: that they know Thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom Thou didst send.

relationship: related resistance to manufactured likenesses
rationale: Wisdom says human inventions and painted forms did not mislead God's people; Deuteronomy likewise warns against turning the unseen God into a manufactured likeness.
source_text: For neither the evil-devising invention of human beings misled us, nor the fruitless labor of painters, a form stained with varied colors,

target_units.text: And you shall guard your souls diligently; for you saw no likeness in the day when the Lord spoke unto you in Horeb, on the mountain, out of the midst of the fire,
lest you act lawlessly and make for yourselves a graven likeness, any image, the likeness of male or female,

relationship: internal contrast of attractive finish and lifelessness
rationale: The desired, colored image has no breath; the earlier portrait likewise describes an image painted attractively yet incapable of giving life or movement.
source_text: the sight of which stirs desire in fools, and one longs for the breathless form of a dead image.

target_units.text: or made it like some worthless animal, coating it with red ocher and reddening its surface with paint, and covering every blemish in it,
and made for it a dwelling worthy of it, set it in a wall, and secured it with iron.
He took care that it would not fall, knowing that it cannot help itself; for it is an image and needs help.
Yet when praying concerning his possessions, marriage, and children, he is not ashamed to address what has no soul; for health he calls upon what is weak,
for life he petitions what is dead, for assistance he begs what is utterly inexperienced, for a journey what cannot even use its feet,

relationship: parallel joined assessment of idol-makers and worshipers
rationale: Wisdom joins the makers, desirers and worshipers in blame; the psalm likewise joins makers and those trusting idols in their fate.
source_text: Lovers of evil and worthy of such hopes are those who make them, those who desire them, and those who worship them.

target_units.text: May those who make them become like them, and all who have put their trust in them.

relationship: close potter and differing-vessels analogy
rationale: Both describe a potter making vessels for differing uses from the same material; Wisdom discusses clean and opposite uses, while Romans speaks of honor and dishonor within an analogy about God.
source_text: For a potter, laboriously kneading soft earth, shapes each object for our service; from the same clay he fashioned alike vessels serving clean purposes and those serving the opposite; and the clay-worker decides the use of each kind.

target_units.text: Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

relationship: close earth-origin and earth-return formula
rationale: The mortal potter will return to the earth from which he was taken, closely recalling the sentence that humanity is earth and returns to earth.
source_text: With evil labor he also shapes a futile god from the same clay, though he himself, having come from earth a little before, will shortly go back to that from which he was taken, when the debt of his soul is demanded.

target_units.text: By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for earth you are, and unto earth you shall return.

relationship: parallel rivalry driving skilled labor
rationale: The potter competes with metalworkers and prizes his imitations; Ecclesiastes likewise identifies rivalry with one's companion within toil and courage in work.
source_text: But his concern is not that he is about to die, nor that his life is short; instead, he competes with goldsmiths and silver-workers, imitates bronze-workers, and considers it glory that he fashions counterfeits.

target_units.text: I saw all toil and all courage in work: it is a person’s rivalry with his companion. This too is futility and resolve of spirit.

relationship: close ashes-heart criticism of idol-making
rationale: Wisdom calls the idol-maker's heart ashes; Isaiah likewise says the heart of those manufacturing and worshiping idols is ashes.
source_text: His heart is ashes, and his hope more worthless than earth, and his life more dishonorable than clay,

target_units.text: Know that their heart is ashes, and they wander, and no one can rescue his soul. See—will you not say, ‘A lie is in my right hand’?

relationship: close divine-breath creation allusion
rationale: The unknown true Maker breathes an active soul and life-giving spirit into the person; Genesis likewise narrates God's breath of life and the human becoming a living soul.
source_text: because he did not know the One who formed him, who breathed into him an active soul and breathed in a life-giving spirit.

target_units.text: And God formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

relationship: related commercial pride about brief human life
rationale: Wisdom condemns reducing existence to a profitable fair; James likewise rebukes confident plans to trade and profit while ignoring life's vapor-like brevity and God's will.
source_text: Instead, they reckoned our life a plaything and our existence a profitable fair; for he says that one must make gain from whatever source, even evil.

target_units.text: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this city, spend a year there, trade, and make a profit”—
you who do not know what tomorrow brings. What is your life? For you are a vapor, appearing for a little while and then disappearing.
Instead, you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we shall both live and do this or that.”
But now you boast in your pretensions. All such boasting is evil.

relationship: internal recurrence of infant-like religious folly
rationale: The oppressors are judged more wretched than an infant's soul; the earlier passage likewise describes animal-worshipers as deceived like senseless infants.
source_text: But all the enemies of Thy people who oppressed them are most foolish and more wretched than an infant’s soul,

target_units.text: For they wandered even farther than the paths of error, supposing that creatures despised even among shameful animals were gods, deceived like senseless infants.

relationship: close catalogue of idols' unusable senses
rationale: Both list idols' eyes, ears, noses, hands and feet while denying their ability to see, hear, perceive or walk.
source_text: because they also reckoned all the nations’ idols gods, though these have neither use of eyes for sight, nor nostrils for drawing in air, nor ears to hear, nor fingers of their hands to feel, and their feet are idle for walking.

target_units.text: They have a mouth and will not speak; they have eyes and will not see.
They have ears and will not hear; they have noses and will not smell.
They have hands and will not feel; feet, and will not walk; they will not sound with their throat.

relationship: contrast of borrowed life with the life-giving Creator
rationale: Wisdom contrasts a spirit-borrowing human maker with true divinity; Acts likewise says God gives life and breath and cannot be equated with a humanly formed image.
source_text: For a human being made them, and one who had borrowed his spirit fashioned them; for no human being can shape a god like himself.

target_units.text: Nor is He served by human hands as though He needed anything, since He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything.
From one He made every nation of humanity to live upon the whole face of the earth, determining their appointed times and the boundaries of their dwelling,
so that they might seek God, if perhaps they might feel their way toward Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us.
For in Him we live and move and exist, as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we too are His offspring.’
Since we are God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine nature is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by human art and thought.

relationship: parallel lifelessness of manufactured gods
rationale: Wisdom distinguishes living mortal makers from their dead products; Jeremiah likewise says fabricated images are false and have no spirit in them.
source_text: Being mortal, he makes a dead thing with lawless hands; for he is better than the objects he worships: he at least has lived, but they never have.

target_units.text: Every human became foolish, without knowledge; every goldsmith was put to shame at his carved things, because they cast false things; there is no spirit in them.

relationship: parallel animal-directed idolatry
rationale: Wisdom condemns worship of irrational animals; Romans similarly describes the exchange of divine glory for images of birds, quadrupeds and creeping things.
source_text: They also worship the most hateful animals, for compared in senselessness with the others, these are worse;

target_units.text: and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible humanity, and of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things.

relationship: contrast in evaluation of animals
rationale: Wisdom denies praise and blessing to the animals treated as gods; Genesis calls the created animals good. The comparison preserves these different evaluations rather than assuming identical objects of praise.
source_text: Nor, in their appearance as animals, are they beautiful enough to be desired, and they have escaped both God’s praise and His blessing.

target_units.text: And God said, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kind: four-footed animals, creeping things, and wild beasts of the earth according to their kind.” And it was so.

And God made the wild beasts of the earth according to their kind, and the cattle according to their kind, and all the creeping things of the earth according to their kinds. And God saw that they were good.

relationship: animal-plague narrative background
rationale: The oppressors' torment through beasts corresponds to the threatened dog-flies in Egyptian homes, contrasted with Israel's protection in Goshen.
source_text: Therefore they were deservedly punished through similar creatures and tormented by a multitude of beasts.

target_units.text: But if you will not let My people go, behold, I will send dog-flies upon you, and upon your attendants, and upon your people, and upon your houses; and the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with dog-flies, and also the ground on which they stand.
And in that day I will marvellously distinguish the land of Goshen, in which My people dwell, so that no dog-flies shall be there; that you may know that I am the Lord, the Lord of all the earth.
And I will put a distinction between My people and your people; tomorrow this sign shall be upon the land.’”

relationship: quail-provision narrative allusion
rationale: Wisdom's beneficial quail food corresponds to the Lord's promise of meat and the quail covering Israel's camp.
source_text: In contrast to that punishment, Thou didst benefit Thy people: to meet their eager appetite Thou didst prepare quail as food, a novel taste,

target_units.text: “I have heard the sons of Israel’s murmuring. Tell them: Toward evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall have your fill of bread. You shall know that I am the Lord your God.”
Evening came, and quail came up and covered the camp. In the morning, as the dew around the camp was subsiding,

relationship: internal contrast of punitive creatures and desired food
rationale: The contrast between repellent creatures and quail nourishment is recalled later through the production of gnats and frogs alongside quail satisfying the people's desire.
source_text: so that those, though desiring food, would turn away even from their necessary appetite because of the loathsomeness of the creatures sent upon them, while these, after a brief lack, would share in a novel taste.

target_units.text: For they still remembered the things from their sojourn: how, instead of producing animals, the earth brought forth gnats, and instead of aquatic creatures the river disgorged a multitude of frogs.
Later they also saw a new production of birds, when, urged on by desire, they asked for luxurious foods;
for as a consolation quail came up to them from the sea.

relationship: internal distinction of instructional trial and hostile judgment
rationale: Israel's brief lack shows how enemies are tormented; the earlier account likewise says merciful testing taught Israel how the ungodly suffered judgment.
source_text: For unavoidable need had to come upon those who oppressed, but these only had to be shown how their enemies were tormented.

target_units.text: For when they were tested, although disciplined in mercy, they learned how the ungodly were tormented when judged in wrath.

relationship: serpent-plague and remedy allusion
rationale: The deadly snake attack followed by limited wrath corresponds to the serpents' bites and the remedy God gave through Moses.
source_text: For even when the terrible fury of beasts came upon them, and they were being destroyed by the bites of twisting snakes, Thy wrath did not remain to the end;

target_units.text: And the Lord sent deadly serpents among the people. They bit the people, and many of the sons of Israel died.

And the people came unto Moses and said: We have sinned by speaking against the Lord and against you. Therefore pray unto the Lord, and let Him remove the serpents from us. Moses prayed unto the Lord for the people.
And the Lord said unto Moses: Make a serpent for yourself, and set it upon a standard; and it shall be, if a serpent bites a man, that everyone bitten, when he looks upon it, shall live.
And Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a standard. Whenever a serpent bit a person, that person looked at the bronze serpent and lived.

relationship: salvation-symbol narrative allusion
rationale: The short admonition's visible symbol recalls the serpent placed on a standard at God's command, toward which the bitten could look and live.
source_text: they were troubled for a short time as an admonition, having a symbol of salvation to remind them of the commandment of Thy law.

target_units.text: And the Lord said unto Moses: Make a serpent for yourself, and set it upon a standard; and it shall be, if a serpent bites a man, that everyone bitten, when he looks upon it, shall live.
And Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a standard. Whenever a serpent bit a person, that person looked at the bronze serpent and lived.

relationship: interpretation of the serpent remedy
rationale: Wisdom attributes rescue to God rather than the visible object; Numbers supplies the commanded looking and resulting life, while Wisdom states the theological explanation.
source_text: For the one who turned toward it was saved not through what was seen, but through Thee, the Savior of all.

target_units.text: And the Lord said unto Moses: Make a serpent for yourself, and set it upon a standard; and it shall be, if a serpent bites a man, that everyone bitten, when he looks upon it, shall live.
And Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a standard. Whenever a serpent bit a person, that person looked at the bronze serpent and lived.

relationship: parallel confidence in rescue from every evil
rationale: The source names God as the One rescuing from every evil; Paul likewise expresses confidence that the Lord will rescue him from every evil work.
source_text: Through this Thou didst also convince our enemies that Thou art the One who rescues from every evil.

target_units.text: The Lord will rescue me from every evil work and save me into His heavenly kingdom. To Him be glory for the ages of ages. Amen.

relationship: related destructive-insect plague tradition
rationale: Wisdom describes fatal insect bites; the psalm likewise says a dog-fly devoured the Egyptians and locusts received their labors. It supports destructive insect judgment without specifying Wisdom's full account of fatal locust bites.
source_text: For the bites of locusts and flies killed those others, and no cure was found for their lives, because they deserved to be punished by such creatures;

target_units.text: He sent a dog-fly among them, and it devoured them, and a frog, and it destroyed them.
And He gave their fruit to mildew, and their labors to the locust.

relationship: serpent-remedy and survival allusion
rationale: The serpents fail to overcome God's sons because mercy heals them; Numbers likewise reports bitten people looking at the bronze serpent and living.
source_text: but even the teeth of venom-spitting serpents did not conquer Thy sons, for Thy mercy came to meet them and healed them.

target_units.text: And Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a standard. Whenever a serpent bit a person, that person looked at the bronze serpent and lived.

relationship: narrative basis for remedial serpent discipline
rationale: The bites lead to renewed attention and rescue; Numbers similarly records confession, Moses's prayer and obedience to God's remedy, without explicitly stating Wisdom's warning about future forgetfulness.
source_text: For they were stung as a reminder of Thine oracles and swiftly brought safely through, so that they would not fall into deep forgetfulness and become inattentive to Thy beneficence.

target_units.text: And the people came unto Moses and said: We have sinned by speaking against the Lord and against you. Therefore pray unto the Lord, and let Him remove the serpents from us. Moses prayed unto the Lord for the people.
And the Lord said unto Moses: Make a serpent for yourself, and set it upon a standard; and it shall be, if a serpent bites a man, that everyone bitten, when he looks upon it, shall live.
And Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a standard. Whenever a serpent bit a person, that person looked at the bronze serpent and lived.

relationship: close divine-word healing motif
rationale: Wisdom locates healing in God's word rather than a medicine; the psalm likewise says God sent His word, healed the afflicted and rescued them.
source_text: For neither herb nor poultice healed them, but Thy word, Lord, which heals all.

target_units.text: He sent His word and healed them and rescued them from their destructions.

relationship: close life-death and Hades authority formula
rationale: Both declare God's power to put to death or give life and to bring down to Hades and bring up again.
source_text: For Thou hast authority over life and death, and Thou bringest down to the gates of Hades and bringest up again;

target_units.text: The Lord puts to death and gives life; He brings down to Hades and brings up.

relationship: parallel human inability to control death and spirit
rationale: Wisdom denies human ability to restore a departed spirit; Ecclesiastes similarly denies human authority to restrain the spirit or govern the day of death.
source_text: but a human being kills by his wickedness, and does not bring back a spirit that has gone out, nor release a soul that has been taken.

target_units.text: No human being has authority over the spirit to restrain the spirit, and there is no authority over the day of death. There is no discharge in war, and ungodliness will not rescue the one who possesses it.

relationship: close inescapable-divine-hand formula
rationale: Wisdom says escape from God's hand is impossible; Deuteronomy likewise declares that none can deliver out of His hands.
source_text: But it is impossible to escape Thy hand.

target_units.text: See, see that I am, and there is no god beside Me. I will put to death, and make alive; I will smite, and I will heal; and there is none that shall deliver out of My hands.

relationship: hail-and-fire plague allusion
rationale: The ungodly pursued by hail, showers and fire recall the thunder, hail and fire that devastated Egypt's people and produce.
source_text: For the ungodly, refusing to know Thee, were scourged by the strength of Thine arm, pursued by strange rains, hail, and relentless showers, and consumed by fire.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven. The Lord sent thunder and hail, and fire ran over the earth. The Lord rained hail upon all the land of Egypt.
There was hail, with fire flaming amid the hail. The hail was very, very abundant, such as had never been in Egypt since a nation came to be there.
Throughout Egypt the hail struck people and livestock. It struck every plant in the plains and shattered all the trees there.

relationship: interpretation of fire amid hail
rationale: Wisdom marvels at fire operating in water; Exodus supplies the fire flaming amid hail, without explicitly explaining it as fire exceeding its natural power.
source_text: Most astonishingly, in water that quenches everything, the fire worked still more strongly, for the world fights for the righteous.

target_units.text: There was hail, with fire flaming amid the hail. The hail was very, very abundant, such as had never been in Egypt since a nation came to be there.

relationship: internal recurrence of fire sparing living creatures
rationale: The tamed flame that does not consume the punitive animals is recalled in the final account of flames not withering perishable animals walking among them.
source_text: At one time the flame was tamed, so that it would not burn up the animals sent against the ungodly, but they themselves, seeing, would know that they were being driven by God’s judgment;

target_units.text: flames, conversely, did not wither the flesh of perishable animals walking among them, nor the meltable, crystal-like kind of heavenly food that readily melts.

relationship: plague destruction of produce
rationale: The fire that destroys the unrighteous land's produce belongs to the plague whose hail struck Egypt's plants and shattered its trees.
source_text: at another time, even amid water, it burns beyond fire’s own power, so that it may destroy the produce of an unrighteous land.

target_units.text: Throughout Egypt the hail struck people and livestock. It struck every plant in the plains and shattered all the trees there.

relationship: close heavenly and angelic bread description
rationale: Wisdom calls the provided food angels' food and bread from heaven; the psalm likewise calls manna heaven's bread and angels' bread.
source_text: In contrast, Thou didst feed Thy people with angels’ food and supply them ready bread from heaven without toil, capable of every delight and suited to every taste.

target_units.text: And He commanded the clouds above and opened heaven’s doors,
and rained manna for them to eat, and gave them heaven’s bread.
A man ate angels’ bread; He sent them food supplies to fullness.

relationship: manna-taste narrative background
rationale: Wisdom expands the nourishing food's sweetness into adaptation to each desired taste; Exodus describes manna's honey-cake taste but not that transformation.
source_text: For Thy sustenance manifested Thy sweetness toward Thy children; serving the desire of the one who received it, it was transformed into whatever that person wished.

target_units.text: The sons of Israel called it Man. It was like coriander seed, white, and tasted like a cake with honey.

relationship: fire-and-hail background of the paradox
rationale: Wisdom interprets enduring ice and snow beside destructive fire; Exodus reports fire flaming amid hail, without spelling out the same physical explanation.
source_text: Snow and ice endured fire and did not melt, so that they might know that the enemies’ fruits were destroyed by fire blazing in the hail and flashing in the rains;

target_units.text: There was hail, with fire flaming amid the hail. The hail was very, very abundant, such as had never been in Egypt since a nation came to be there.

relationship: internal recurrence of fire sparing heavenly food
rationale: The fire forgets its destructive power so that the righteous may be nourished; this corresponds to the final statement that flames did not wither the meltable heavenly food.
source_text: yet again, so that the righteous might be nourished, this fire has even forgotten its own power.

target_units.text: flames, conversely, did not wither the flesh of perishable animals walking among them, nor the meltable, crystal-like kind of heavenly food that readily melts.

relationship: parallel creation obeying its Maker
rationale: Wisdom describes creation adjusting to God's purposes; the psalm likewise names fire, hail, snow, ice and storm wind as fulfilling His word.
source_text: For creation, serving Thee who made it, strains itself for punishment against the unrighteous and relaxes itself for benefit on behalf of those who trust in Thee.

target_units.text: Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps,
fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind—all fulfilling His word,

relationship: internal account of creation's adaptable service
rationale: The nourishing gift is served by creation changing into all things; the concluding account describes elements being rearranged through an analogy with changing harp notes.
source_text: Therefore at that time also, changing into all things, it served Thy gift that nourishes all, according to the desire of those in need,

target_units.text: For the elements were being rearranged among themselves, as notes on a harp change the pattern of the rhythm, while always retaining their sound; this can be inferred precisely from observing what happened.

relationship: close nourishment-by-divine-utterance teaching
rationale: Wisdom interprets the food as teaching that God's utterance preserves humanity; Deuteronomy likewise interprets manna as teaching life by every word from God's mouth rather than bread alone.
source_text: so that Thy sons whom Thou didst love, Lord, might learn that it is not the production of fruits that nourishes a human being, but Thine utterance that preserves those who trust in Thee.

target_units.text: And He afflicted you, and made you hunger, and fed you with manna, which your fathers did not know, that He might declare unto you that man shall not live by bread alone, but man shall live by every word that proceeds through the mouth of God.

relationship: close manna-melting-in-sunlight allusion
rationale: The heavenly food melts under a ray of sun; Exodus likewise says the gathered manna melted when the sun grew hot.
source_text: For what was not destroyed by fire melted when merely warmed by a brief ray of the sun,

target_units.text: They gathered it morning by morning, each what he needed. When the sun grew hot, it melted.

relationship: parallel early appeal to God
rationale: Wisdom draws a lesson of thanksgiving before sunrise; the psalm likewise addresses God in a rising-at-dawn appeal of longing.
source_text: so that it might be known that one must rise before the sun to give Thee thanks and appeal to Thee at the rising of the light.

target_units.text: God, my God, toward Thee I rise at dawn; my soul thirsted for Thee. How greatly my flesh longs for Thee in a desert, trackless and waterless land!

relationship: internal comparison of failed hope to frost
rationale: The ungrateful person's hope melts like frost; the earlier passage likewise compares ungodly hope to fine frost driven by a storm, with a different mode of disappearance.
source_text: For the hope of an ungrateful person will melt like wintry frost and flow away like useless water.

target_units.text: For the hope of an ungodly person is like dust borne by wind, and like fine frost driven by a storm; like smoke it was dispersed by wind, and like the memory of a guest who stayed one day it passed away.

relationship: close immeasurable-divine-judgments motif
rationale: Wisdom calls God's judgments great and hard to recount; Paul likewise calls His judgments unsearchable and His ways untraceable.
source_text: For Thy judgments are great and hard to recount; therefore uninstructed souls went astray.

target_units.text: O depth of God’s wealth and wisdom and knowledge! How unsearchable His judgments and untraceable His ways!

relationship: darkness-plague narrative allusion
rationale: The oppressors' confinement in a long night corresponds to Egypt's three days of darkness, when people could not see one another or rise from bed.
source_text: For lawless people, supposing they could oppress a holy nation, lay as prisoners of darkness and captives of a long night, shut under their roofs, fugitives from eternal providence.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was darkness, gloom, and a tempest throughout the land of Egypt for three days.
No one saw his brother for three days, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the sons of Israel had light everywhere they lived.

relationship: contrast of attempted concealment and divine vision
rationale: The lawless imagine darkness can hide secret sins; the psalm instead declares that darkness does not conceal anything from God.
source_text: For thinking they could escape notice in secret sins, under a lightless covering of forgetfulness, they were scattered, terribly astonished and shaken by apparitions.

target_units.text: And I said, “Then darkness will trample me, and night is light in my delight.”
For darkness will not be dark from Thee, and night will be lit up like day; as its darkness, so also its light.

relationship: expanded description of Egypt's darkness
rationale: The failure of ordinary lights elaborates the narrative of tangible darkness over Egypt; Exodus records the darkness but not the separate failure of fire and stars.
source_text: No force of fire could give light, nor could the bright flames of stars endure to illuminate that hateful night.

target_units.text: And the Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and let there be darkness upon the land of Egypt, darkness that may be felt.”
Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was darkness, gloom, and a tempest throughout the land of Egypt for three days.
No one saw his brother for three days, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the sons of Israel had light everywhere they lived.

relationship: related exposure of Egyptian magic's limits
rationale: Wisdom describes magical claims collapsing; Exodus supplies the magicians' failure to produce gnats and acknowledgment of God's finger, a related episode rather than an assertion that it occurred during the darkness.
source_text: The delusions of magical art lay prostrate, and its boasting of understanding suffered a scornful exposure;

target_units.text: The enchanters tried by their sorceries to bring forth gnats, but they could not. The gnats were on people and four-footed animals.
The enchanters said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God.” But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said.

relationship: parallel disproportionate terror under judgment
rationale: Wisdom depicts people trembling at passing animals and hissing; Leviticus likewise depicts cowardice in which a wind-blown leaf's sound provokes flight without a pursuer.
source_text: For even if nothing disturbing frightened them, startled by the passing of beasts and the hissing of creeping things, they perished trembling, refusing even to look at the air, which cannot be escaped anywhere.

target_units.text: And upon those who remain of you I will bring cowardice into their heart in the land of their enemies; and the sound of a leaf borne along shall pursue them; and they shall flee as those fleeing from war, and fall when none pursues;

relationship: parallel accusing conscience
rationale: Wickedness condemns itself through conscience here; Romans likewise speaks of conscience bearing witness and inner reasonings accusing before God's judgment.
source_text: For wickedness is a cowardly thing, condemned by its own witness; pressed by conscience, it always imagines grievous things.

target_units.text: who show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness with it, and their reasonings among themselves accusing or even defending,
on the day when God judges people’s secrets according to my gospel through Christ Jesus.

relationship: darkness-plague background of helpless rest
rationale: The common helpless night recalls Egypt's darkness and inability to rise from bed; Wisdom's description of its origin in Hades goes beyond Exodus's narration.
source_text: But they, sleeping the same sleep during that truly powerless night, which had come upon them from the recesses of powerless Hades,

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was darkness, gloom, and a tempest throughout the land of Egypt for three days.
No one saw his brother for three days, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the sons of Israel had light everywhere they lived.

relationship: related frightening nocturnal experience
rationale: Wisdom describes apparitions and sudden paralyzing fear; Eliphaz likewise recounts nocturnal terrors, trembling and an unrecognized spiritual presence, in a different setting.
source_text: were at one moment driven by monstrous apparitions, at another paralyzed by their soul’s betrayal; for a sudden and unexpected fear poured over them.

target_units.text: There were terrors and a nocturnal sound, fear falling upon people;
a shudder and trembling met me and shook my bones greatly.
A spirit came upon my face, and my hair and flesh shuddered.
I stood up and did not recognize it; I looked, and there was no form before my eyes, but I heard a breeze and a voice:

relationship: parallel confinement without physical bonds
rationale: The person becomes a prisoner without iron bars; Exodus similarly describes the darkness preventing people from rising from their beds.
source_text: Then whoever it might be who fell there was held under guard, shut in a prison without iron bars.

target_units.text: No one saw his brother for three days, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the sons of Israel had light everywhere they lived.

relationship: parallel comprehensive restraint by darkness
rationale: Wisdom's workers of every occupation share one chain of darkness; Exodus likewise reports general Egyptian darkness and immobility, without enumerating occupations.
source_text: For whether someone was a farmer or shepherd or a laborer toiling in the wilderness, once overtaken, he endured the inescapable compulsion; for all were bound by one chain of darkness.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was darkness, gloom, and a tempest throughout the land of Egypt for three days.
No one saw his brother for three days, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the sons of Israel had light everywhere they lived.

relationship: related sounds provoking fearful flight
rationale: The wind, birds, water and rocks belong to Wisdom's catalogue of terror-producing sounds; Leviticus likewise makes the sound of a moving leaf occasion cowardly flight.
source_text: Whether a whistling wind, or the melodious sound of birds among spreading branches, or the rhythm of water rushing violently, or the harsh crash of falling rocks,

target_units.text: And upon those who remain of you I will bring cowardice into their heart in the land of their enemies; and the sound of a leaf borne along shall pursue them; and they shall flee as those fleeing from war, and fall when none pursues;

relationship: parallel fear exceeding any pursuing enemy
rationale: Unseen movement, roars and echoes paralyze the people; Leviticus similarly describes flight and collapse even though no enemy pursues.
source_text: or the unseen running of leaping animals, or the voice of the fiercest roaring beasts, or an echo rebounding from the hollows of mountains, these terrified and paralyzed them.

target_units.text: And upon those who remain of you I will bring cowardice into their heart in the land of their enemies; and the sound of a leaf borne along shall pursue them; and they shall flee as those fleeing from war, and fall when none pursues;
and brother shall disregard brother as in war, though no one runs after them. You shall not be able to withstand your enemies.

relationship: contrast between darkness's victims and those in light
rationale: Wisdom contrasts the afflicted region with the illuminated world; Exodus likewise contrasts Egyptian darkness with light where Israel lived, without making the broader worldwide statement.
source_text: For the whole world was illuminated by brilliant light and occupied with unhindered works;

target_units.text: No one saw his brother for three days, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the sons of Israel had light everywhere they lived.

relationship: Egyptian darkness interpreted as judgment
rationale: The heavy night over the oppressors alone develops Exodus's contrast between Egypt's darkness and Israel's light; Wisdom adds its image of future darkness and inward burden.
source_text: but over those alone a heavy night was spread, an image of the darkness that was to receive them; yet they were heavier to themselves than the darkness.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was darkness, gloom, and a tempest throughout the land of Egypt for three days.
No one saw his brother for three days, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the sons of Israel had light everywhere they lived.

relationship: close light-for-Israel contrast
rationale: The holy ones' great light corresponds to Israel having light where they lived while Egyptians could not see one another.
source_text: But for Thy holy ones there was very great light; hearing their voices but not seeing their forms, the others called them blessed because they had not suffered likewise,

target_units.text: No one saw his brother for three days, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the sons of Israel had light everywhere they lived.

relationship: ethical parallel of refusing retaliation
rationale: The previously injured holy ones do not harm their opponents; Paul likewise commands no repayment of evil for evil and overcoming evil with good.
source_text: and thanked them because, though previously wronged, they did not harm them, and begged pardon for their quarrel.

target_units.text: Repay no one evil for evil. Take thought for what is honorable before all people.
If possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people.
Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but make room for wrath; for it is written, “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.”
But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head.
Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.

relationship: fire-pillar guidance allusion
rationale: The blazing pillar guiding the unknown journey corresponds to the fire pillar by which God led Israel at night.
source_text: In contrast, Thou didst supply a fire-blazing pillar, a guide for an unknown journey, and a harmless sun for a glorious sojourn abroad.

target_units.text: God led them by day in a pillar of cloud to show them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire.
The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not cease before all the people.

relationship: related worldwide mission of Israel's law
rationale: Wisdom says the sons kept captive were to mediate law's light to the world; Isaiah likewise depicts nations seeking instruction as law goes out from Zion.
source_text: For those deserved to be deprived of light and imprisoned in darkness who had kept Thy sons shut up, through whom the incorruptible light of law was to be given to the world.

target_units.text: In the last days the Lord’s mountain and God’s house will be clearly visible on the summits of the mountains and be raised above the hills; all the nations will come to it,

and many nations will go and say, “Come, let us go up to the Lord’s mountain and to the house of Jacob’s God. He will announce His way to us, and we will walk in it.” For law will go out from Zion, and the Lord’s word from Jerusalem.

relationship: background of the planned destruction of Hebrew infants
rationale: Wisdom interprets the later Egyptian deaths against the plan to kill Israel's infants; Exodus supplies Pharaoh's command to cast the Hebrew boys into the river.
source_text: When they planned to kill the infants of the holy ones, and one child had been exposed and saved, Thou didst take away their multitude of children as a rebuke and destroy them together in violent water.

target_units.text: And Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, “Cast every male child born to the Hebrews into the river, but keep every female child alive.”

relationship: patriarchal promise behind expected deliverance
rationale: Wisdom recalls ancestral assurance before the saving night; Genesis records the prior covenant announcement of foreign oppression, judgment upon the oppressing nation and the descendants' departure, without naming Passover's date.
source_text: That night was known beforehand to our fathers, so that, knowing securely the oaths in which they trusted, they might take courage.

target_units.text: And it was said to Abram, “Know for certain that your seed shall live as strangers in a land not their own; and they shall enslave them, and afflict them, and humble them for four hundred years.
But I will judge the nation they serve; and afterward they shall come out here with much baggage.
But you shall depart to your fathers in peace, buried at a good old age.
And in the fourth generation they shall return here; for the sins of the Amorites are not yet filled up.”
And as the sun was setting, a flame appeared; and behold, a smoking furnace, and torches of fire which passed between these divided pieces.

relationship: Passover expectation of judgment and protection
rationale: The people await the salvation of the righteous and enemies' destruction; Exodus announces the same night's striking of Egypt and sheltering of marked Israelite houses.
source_text: Thy people awaited the salvation of the righteous and the destruction of enemies;

target_units.text: I will go through the land of Egypt that night and strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both human and animal. Against all the Egyptians’ gods I will execute vengeance. I am the Lord.
And the blood shall be a sign to you upon the houses in which you are; and I will see the blood, and shelter you; and no plague of destruction shall be among you when I strike the land of Egypt.

relationship: one event bringing judgment and protection
rationale: Wisdom's punishment of opponents and glorification of God's people correspond to the Passover night that strikes Egypt while preventing destruction in Israel's houses.
source_text: for by the very means through which Thou didst punish the opponents, Thou didst glorify us, calling us to Thyself.

target_units.text: I will go through the land of Egypt that night and strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both human and animal. Against all the Egyptians’ gods I will execute vengeance. I am the Lord.
And the blood shall be a sign to you upon the houses in which you are; and I will see the blood, and shelter you; and no plague of destruction shall be among you when I strike the land of Egypt.

relationship: communal Passover-sacrifice background
rationale: The holy families' united sacrifice recalls the household allocation and whole congregation's slaughter of the Passover animal; Exodus does not supply the same account of ancestral hymns.
source_text: For in secret the holy children of good ancestors offered sacrifice, and in unity established the divine law: that the saints would share alike in the same good things and dangers, already singing beforehand the praises of the fathers.

target_units.text: Speak to the whole congregation of the sons of Israel, saying: On the tenth day of this month, each shall take a sheep for the ancestral households, one sheep for each household.

If those in the house are too few to be sufficient for a sheep, he shall join with his nearest neighbour. According to the number of persons, each person’s sufficient portion shall be reckoned for the sheep.
Your sheep shall be without blemish, a male a year old; you shall take it from the lambs and from the young goats.
And you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month; and the whole multitude of the congregation of the sons of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening.
They shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat them.
They shall eat the meat that night, roasted over fire, and eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs.

relationship: close Egyptian cry after firstborn deaths
rationale: Wisdom's pitiful mourning cry corresponds to the great cry through Egypt because every household had a dead person.
source_text: But the discordant cry of enemies echoed back, and a pitiful sound spread abroad as children were mourned.

target_units.text: Pharaoh rose during the night, with all his attendants and all the Egyptians. There was a great cry throughout the land of Egypt, for there was no house without someone dead.

relationship: close judgment across social ranks
rationale: Wisdom joins slave, master, commoner and king in one judgment; Exodus likewise ranges from Pharaoh's firstborn to the captive woman's firstborn.
source_text: Slave and master were punished together by the same judgment, and the commoner suffered the same things as the king;

target_units.text: At midnight the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on the throne to the firstborn of the captive woman in the pit, and the firstborn of every animal of the livestock.

relationship: firstborn-death narrative background
rationale: The simultaneous loss of honored offspring corresponds to the midnight striking and widespread bereavement; Wisdom adds the claim that survivors could not bury all the dead.
source_text: all together, under one name of death, they had countless dead; for the living were not even sufficient to bury them, since in a single moment their most honored offspring had been destroyed.

target_units.text: At midnight the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on the throne to the firstborn of the captive woman in the pit, and the firstborn of every animal of the livestock.
Pharaoh rose during the night, with all his attendants and all the Egyptians. There was a great cry throughout the land of Egypt, for there was no house without someone dead.

relationship: close Israel-as-son and firstborn-judgment connection
rationale: Wisdom ties recognition of God's son to the firstborn's destruction; Exodus already links Israel as God's firstborn son with the threatened death of Pharaoh's firstborn.
source_text: For though they disbelieved everything because of their sorceries, at the destruction of the firstborn they acknowledged that the people were God’s son.

target_units.text: And you shall say to Pharaoh, ‘Thus says the Lord: Israel is My firstborn son.
And I said to you, “Let My people go, that they may serve Me.” If therefore you will not let them go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son.’”

relationship: midnight-judgment allusion
rationale: Wisdom's silence halfway through the night sets the judgment scene that Exodus explicitly locates at midnight.
source_text: For while quiet silence surrounded all things and night was midway through its swift course,

target_units.text: At midnight the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on the throne to the firstborn of the captive woman in the pit, and the firstborn of every animal of the livestock.

relationship: related divine-word and sword imagery
rationale: Wisdom portrays God's commanded judgment through an armed, sword-bearing word; Hebrews likewise likens God's active, judging word to a penetrating sword, without identifying this Egyptian judgment as the incarnation.
source_text: Thine all-powerful word leaped from heaven, from royal thrones, a stern warrior, into the midst of the doomed land, carrying Thine unfeigned command as a sharp sword;

target_units.text: For the word of God is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword, penetrating as far as the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
And no created thing is hidden before Him, but all things are naked and laid open to His eyes, to whom we must give account.

relationship: firstborn judgment behind the cosmic-warrior image
rationale: The word filling the land with death interprets the Lord's midnight striking of Egypt; Exodus does not narrate the heaven-touching warrior's stature.
source_text: standing there, it filled all things with death; it touched heaven while standing upon the earth.

target_units.text: At midnight the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on the throne to the firstborn of the captive woman in the pit, and the firstborn of every animal of the livestock.

relationship: Israelite outbreak and halted wrath allusion
rationale: The righteous people's brief death trial recalls the outbreak among Israel that ceased after priestly atonement.
source_text: But a trial of death touched the righteous too, and a breaking of the multitude occurred in the wilderness; yet the wrath did not remain long.

target_units.text: Withdraw from the midst of this congregation, and I will consume them all at once. They fell on their faces.

And Moses said unto Aaron: Take the fire pan, put fire from the altar on it, and place incense on it. Carry it quickly into the camp and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from before the Lord; it has begun to strike the people.
And Aaron took it just as Moses had told him and ran into the congregation. The outbreak had already begun among the people. He placed the incense and made atonement for the people,
and stood between the dead and the living, and the outbreak subsided.

relationship: Aaron's incense intercession allusion
rationale: The minister hastening with incense to oppose wrath recalls Aaron running into the congregation with the fire pan and making atonement.
source_text: For a blameless man hastened to fight for them, bringing the weapon of his own ministry: prayer and propitiation by incense. He opposed the wrath and put an end to the calamity, showing that he was Thy servant.

target_units.text: And Moses said unto Aaron: Take the fire pan, put fire from the altar on it, and place incense on it. Carry it quickly into the camp and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from before the Lord; it has begun to strike the people.
And Aaron took it just as Moses had told him and ran into the congregation. The outbreak had already begun among the people. He placed the incense and made atonement for the people,
and stood between the dead and the living, and the outbreak subsided.

relationship: related intercession invoking the fathers' promises
rationale: The priestly appeal to ancestral oaths parallels Moses's distinct intercession recalling God's oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; the two mediators and episodes are not conflated.
source_text: He conquered the anger, not by bodily strength, not by the activity of weapons, but by a word he subdued the punisher, reminding him of the fathers’ oaths and covenants.

target_units.text: Moses entreated the Lord God and said, “Why, O Lord, art Thou angry with Thy people, whom Thou didst lead out of the land of Egypt with great strength and Thine uplifted arm?
Let not the Egyptians say, ‘He led them out with evil intent, to kill them in the mountains and consume them from the earth.’ Cease from Thy fierce anger and be merciful concerning Thy people’s evil,

remembering Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Thy servants, to whom Thou didst swear by Thyself and speak, saying, ‘I will greatly multiply your seed as the stars of heaven in multitude’; and all this land which Thou didst say Thou wouldest give to their seed, they shall possess for ever.”
The Lord was appeased concerning the calamity He had said He would bring upon His people.

relationship: close standing-between-dead-and-living allusion
rationale: Wisdom's mediator stands between the fallen and the living and checks wrath; Numbers explicitly says Aaron stood between dead and living and the outbreak subsided.
source_text: For when the dead had already fallen in heaps upon one another, he stood between them and checked the wrath, and cut off the path to the living.

target_units.text: and stood between the dead and the living, and the outbreak subsided.

relationship: priestly four-row stones background
rationale: The fathers' glories engraved in four rows correspond to the breastpiece's four rows of stones bearing Israel's tribal names; Wisdom supplies its larger cosmic interpretation of the garment.
source_text: For upon his ankle-length garment was the whole world, and the glories of the fathers upon the engraving of four rows of stones, and Thy majesty upon the diadem of his head.

target_units.text: You shall weave into it a fabric set with four rows of stones. The first row shall be a sardius, topaz, and emerald;
the second row a carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper;
the third row a ligure, agate, and amethyst;
the fourth row a chrysolite, beryl, and onyx. They shall be enclosed in gold and bound in gold according to their rows.
The stones shall bear the names of the sons of Israel, twelve according to their names, each engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes.

relationship: halted-outbreak narrative conclusion
rationale: The destroyer's yielding corresponds to the outbreak subsiding after Aaron's intercession; Numbers does not itself attribute this to fear of the priestly ornaments.
source_text: To these the destroyer yielded, and these he feared; for the trial of wrath alone was enough.

target_units.text: and stood between the dead and the living, and the outbreak subsided.
And those who died in the outbreak numbered fourteen thousand seven hundred, apart from those who died because of Korah.
And Aaron returned unto Moses at the entrance of the Tent of Testimony, and the outbreak subsided.

relationship: renewed Egyptian pursuit under divine judgment
rationale: The final fury anticipates the known pursuit; Exodus depicts Pharaoh's hardened heart and renewed pursuit after Israel had departed.
source_text: But merciless fury came upon the ungodly to the end, for He knew beforehand even what they would do,

target_units.text: The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt and of his attendants, and he pursued the sons of Israel. The sons of Israel were going out with a high hand.
The Egyptians pursued them and found them camped by the sea. All Pharaoh’s horse force and chariots, his horsemen, and his army were opposite the settlement, opposite Baal-zephon.

relationship: close change-of-heart and pursuit allusion
rationale: Both recount Egypt reversing its release of Israel and pursuing the departing people.
source_text: that after permitting the people to depart and sending them on their way with haste, they would change their minds and pursue them.

target_units.text: The king of the Egyptians was told that the people had fled. Pharaoh and his attendants had a change of heart toward the people and said, “What have we done, sending the sons of Israel away so that they no longer serve us?”
Pharaoh harnessed his chariots and took all his people with him.
He took six hundred chosen chariots, all the Egyptians’ horse force, and officers over all.
The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt and of his attendants, and he pursued the sons of Israel. The sons of Israel were going out with a high hand.
The Egyptians pursued them and found them camped by the sea. All Pharaoh’s horse force and chariots, his horsemen, and his army were opposite the settlement, opposite Baal-zephon.

relationship: background of mourning and urgent expulsion
rationale: Wisdom stresses the folly of pursuing those just begged to leave; Exodus supplies the mourning cry and urgent Egyptian demand for Israel's departure before the subsequent pursuit.
source_text: For while their griefs were still at hand and they were lamenting beside the graves of the dead, they drew upon themselves another senseless plan, and pursued as fugitives those whom they had begged to leave.

target_units.text: Pharaoh rose during the night, with all his attendants and all the Egyptians. There was a great cry throughout the land of Egypt, for there was no house without someone dead.
And Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron by night, and said to them, “Rise and depart from among my people, both you and the sons of Israel; go, serve the Lord your God, as you say.
Take your sheep and your cattle, and go. Bless me also.”
The Egyptians pressed the people hard to drive them quickly out of the land, for they said, “We are all dying!”

relationship: parallel divine purpose in the final pursuit
rationale: Wisdom interprets the compulsion toward further punishment; Exodus likewise places the Egyptians' renewed entry into danger within God's announced purpose to display His glory, without mentioning forgetfulness.
source_text: For the compulsion they deserved drew them toward this end and cast upon them forgetfulness of what had happened, so that they might fill up the punishment still lacking in their torments,

target_units.text: Behold, I will harden the heart of Pharaoh and of all the Egyptians, and they will enter after them. I will be glorified through Pharaoh and all his army, his chariots, and his horses.
All the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord when I am glorified through Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horses.”

relationship: close contrasting outcomes at the sea
rationale: The people's astonishing passage and enemies' death correspond to Israel walking on dry ground while the returning sea covers Egypt's forces.
source_text: and Thy people might experience an astonishing journey, while those others found an extraordinary death.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and toward daybreak the water returned to its place. The Egyptians fled beneath the water, and the Lord shook the Egyptians into the midst of the sea.
The water returned and covered the chariots, the riders, and all Pharaoh’s force that had entered the sea after them. Not one of them remained.
But the sons of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.

relationship: creation background for the sea-crossing renewal image
rationale: Wisdom calls the elements' service a new fashioning of creation; Genesis's appearance of dry land from gathered water supplies the original creation pattern behind that comparison.
source_text: For the whole creation, in its own kind, was being fashioned anew from the beginning, serving Thy commands, so that Thy children might be guarded unharmed.

target_units.text: And God said, “Let the water beneath heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.” And it was so. And the water beneath heaven was gathered into its gathering places, and the dry land appeared.
And God called the dry land Earth, and the gathered waters He called Seas. And God saw that it was good.

relationship: dry-road-through-the-sea allusion
rationale: Wisdom's dry way out of the sea corresponds to the divided waters and dry ground of Israel's crossing; the grass-bearing plain is Wisdom's additional description.
source_text: The cloud overshadowing the camp was seen, and dry land rising from water that had existed before, an unobstructed way out of the Red Sea, and a grass-bearing plain out of the violent surge;

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. The Lord drove the sea back with a violent south wind all night and made the sea dry. The water was split.
The sons of Israel entered the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.

relationship: collective passage under God's protecting hand
rationale: The sheltered nation passes after seeing wonders; Exodus likewise describes Israel's safe passage and recognition of the Lord's great hand.
source_text: through it those sheltered by Thy hand passed as an entire nation, having seen marvelous wonders.

target_units.text: But the sons of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.
The Lord rescued Israel that day from the Egyptians’ hand, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.
Israel saw the great hand in what the Lord had done to the Egyptians. The people feared the Lord and trusted God and His attendant Moses.

relationship: close horse-like Exodus guidance image
rationale: Wisdom likens the rescued people to grazing horses; Isaiah likewise compares God's guidance through the abyss to a horse in the wilderness and livestock on a plain, without the same leaping-lamb image.
source_text: For they grazed like horses and leaped like lambs, praising Thee, Lord, who rescued them.

target_units.text: He led them through the abyss like a horse through a wilderness, and they did not grow weary.
Like livestock through a plain, a spirit from the Lord came down and guided them. So Thou didst lead Thy people to make Thyself a glorious name.

relationship: close frogs-from-water and gnats-from-earth allusions
rationale: Wisdom recalls abnormal production of frogs from the river and gnats from earth; Exodus describes both the frogs rising from Egypt's waters and the dust becoming gnats.
source_text: For they still remembered the things from their sojourn: how, instead of producing animals, the earth brought forth gnats, and instead of aquatic creatures the river disgorged a multitude of frogs.

target_units.text: And the Lord said to Moses, “Say to Aaron your brother, ‘Stretch out the staff in your hand over the rivers, and over the canals, and over the marshes, and bring up the frogs.’”
Aaron stretched out his hand over Egypt’s waters and brought up the frogs. The frogs were brought up and covered the land of Egypt.
The Egyptian enchanters did the same by their sorceries and brought frogs up over the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, “Pray to the Lord for me, and let Him remove the frogs from me and my people. I will let them go so that they may sacrifice to the Lord.”

And Moses said to Pharaoh, “Appoint a time for me to pray for you, and for your attendants, and for your people, to destroy the frogs from you and from your people and from your houses; only in the river shall they remain.”
And he said, “Tomorrow.” And he answered, “According to your word; that you may know that there is no other except the Lord.
And the frogs shall be removed from you, and from your houses, and from the farmsteads, and from your attendants, and from your people; only in the river shall they remain.”
Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh. Moses cried to the Lord concerning the appointed limit for the frogs, as Pharaoh had set it.
The Lord did as Moses said. The frogs died in the houses, farmsteads, and fields.
They gathered them in heaps upon heaps, and the land stank.
When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, his heart became heavy and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said.

And the Lord said to Moses, “Say to Aaron, ‘Stretch out the staff in your hand, and strike the dust of the earth; and there shall be gnats upon men and upon four-footed animals, and throughout all the land of Egypt.’”
Aaron stretched out the staff in his hand and struck the earth’s dust, and gnats came upon people and four-footed animals. Gnats appeared in all the earth’s dust throughout the land of Egypt.

relationship: background of desire for richer food
rationale: The request for luxurious foods recalls the people's intense craving for meat and dissatisfaction with manna.
source_text: Later they also saw a new production of birds, when, urged on by desire, they asked for luxurious foods;

target_units.text: And the mixed company among them craved intensely, and the sons of Israel also sat down and wept, saying: Who will feed us meat?
We remember the fish we ate in Egypt for nothing, the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic.
But now our life is parched; our eyes see nothing except the manna.

relationship: close quail-from-the-sea allusion
rationale: Wisdom's quail coming from the sea correspond to the wind carrying quail across from the sea into Israel's camp.
source_text: for as a consolation quail came up to them from the sea.

target_units.text: And a wind went out from the Lord and carried quail across from the sea. It cast them upon the camp, a day’s journey on this side and a day’s journey on that side, around the camp, about two cubits above the ground.

relationship: earlier storm-signs background
rationale: The remembered violent thunderbolts correspond to the thunder, hail and fire that earlier struck Egypt; the target does not itself state Wisdom's comparative judgment about hostility to strangers.
source_text: Punishments also came upon the sinners, not without earlier signs in the violence of thunderbolts; for they suffered justly for their own wickedness, since they had practiced a harsher hatred of strangers.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven. The Lord sent thunder and hail, and fire ran over the earth. The Lord rained hail upon all the land of Egypt.
There was hail, with fire flaming amid the hail. The hail was very, very abundant, such as had never been in Egypt since a nation came to be there.

relationship: background of the later enslavement of benefactors
rationale: The latter group enslaving formerly beneficial strangers corresponds to the new Pharaoh who did not know Joseph and Egypt's oppression of Israel. The former hostile hosts remain the distinct Sodom example.
source_text: For the former did not receive unfamiliar visitors when they came, but these enslaved strangers who had benefited them.

target_units.text: And another king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
And he said to his nation, “Behold, the people of the sons of Israel are a great multitude, and are stronger than we are.
Come, therefore, let us deal craftily with them, lest they multiply; and when war befalls us, they also join our adversaries, wage war against us, and leave the land.”
He set overseers of labour over them to afflict them with their work. They built fortified cities for Pharaoh: Pithom, Rameses, and On, which is the City of the Sun.
But the more they humbled them, the more they multiplied and grew exceedingly, exceedingly strong; and the Egyptians loathed the sons of Israel.
The Egyptians oppressed the sons of Israel by force.
They made their lives painful with hard labour in clay and brickmaking, and with all the work in the plains, in every task in which they enslaved them by force.

relationship: judgment on the former hostile hosts
rationale: The announced visitation on the former group corresponds to Sodom's overthrow after the hostile treatment of visitors narrated earlier in Genesis 19, not to Egypt's later enslavement.
source_text: And not only that: there will be a visitation upon the former, since they received foreigners with hostility;

target_units.text: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of the heaven;
and He overthrew those cities, and all the surrounding country, and all that lived in the cities, and all that sprang from the earth.

relationship: contrast between initial welcome and later oppression
rationale: Wisdom recalls that the later enslavers had first received Israel favorably; Genesis supplies Pharaoh's invitation to settle Jacob's family in the best land, before Exodus's oppressive labors.
source_text: but the latter, after receiving with celebrations those who had already shared in the same rights, afflicted them with terrible labors.

target_units.text: And Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Let them live in the land of Goshen; and if you know that there are able men among them, set them over my livestock.” And Jacob and his sons came into Egypt to Joseph; and Pharaoh king of Egypt heard. And Pharaoh spoke to Joseph, saying, “Your father and your brothers have come to you.
“Behold, the land of Egypt is before you; settle your father and your brothers in the best of the land.”

relationship: close blindness-and-doorway comparison
rationale: Wisdom explicitly compares the later darkness with the men at the righteous person's doors; Genesis reports the Sodomites' blindness and inability to find Lot's door.
source_text: They were also struck with blindness, like those at the righteous man’s doors, when, surrounded by yawning darkness, each sought the passage through his own doors.

target_units.text: And they struck the men who were at the door of the house with blindness, from small to great; and they became helpless in seeking the door.

relationship: internal explanation of creation's altered service
rationale: The rearranged elements recapitulate creation stretching or relaxing to serve God's purposes and changing to provide His nourishing gift.
source_text: For the elements were being rearranged among themselves, as notes on a harp change the pattern of the rhythm, while always retaining their sound; this can be inferred precisely from observing what happened.

target_units.text: For creation, serving Thee who made it, strains itself for punishment against the unrighteous and relaxes itself for benefit on behalf of those who trust in Thee.
Therefore at that time also, changing into all things, it served Thy gift that nourishes all, according to the desire of those in need,

relationship: hail-fire narrative basis for reversed elemental behavior
rationale: Wisdom says fire exceeds its power in water; Exodus supplies the concrete combination of fire flaming amid hail, without describing the same change of natural properties.
source_text: fire in water exceeded its own power, and water forgot its nature of extinguishing;

target_units.text: There was hail, with fire flaming amid the hail. The hail was very, very abundant, such as had never been in Egypt since a nation came to be there.

relationship: internal recapitulation of restrained fire
rationale: The spared animals and meltable heavenly food summarize the earlier account of flame withheld from creatures and fire forgetting its power for Israel's nourishment.
source_text: flames, conversely, did not wither the flesh of perishable animals walking among them, nor the meltable, crystal-like kind of heavenly food that readily melts.

target_units.text: At one time the flame was tamed, so that it would not burn up the animals sent against the ungodly, but they themselves, seeing, would know that they were being driven by God’s judgment;
at another time, even amid water, it burns beyond fire’s own power, so that it may destroy the produce of an unrighteous land.
In contrast, Thou didst feed Thy people with angels’ food and supply them ready bread from heaven without toil, capable of every delight and suited to every taste.
For Thy sustenance manifested Thy sweetness toward Thy children; serving the desire of the one who received it, it was transformed into whatever that person wished.
Snow and ice endured fire and did not melt, so that they might know that the enemies’ fruits were destroyed by fire blazing in the hail and flashing in the rains;
yet again, so that the righteous might be nourished, this fire has even forgotten its own power.

relationship: parallel summary of sustained Exodus care
rationale: Wisdom concludes with God's continual support of His people; the psalm similarly summarizes their guidance as a flock through the wilderness, safety from the sea and arrival at their inheritance.
source_text: For in every way, Lord, Thou didst magnify and glorify Thy people, and didst not disregard them, standing beside them at every time and place.

target_units.text: And He led His people away like sheep, and brought them up like a flock in the wilderness,
and guided them in hope, and they did not grow cowardly; and the sea covered their enemies.
And He brought them into the boundary of His sanctuary, this mountain which His right hand acquired,
and expelled nations from before them, and assigned them by a cord of inheritance, and settled Israel’s tribes in their tents.
